assumptions: System A axioms A1-A3
alphabet sizes 2-4
words of bounded length (exact, since the relations preserve length)
new.falsification: Any slice where a class contains two words with different projections, or two words with equal projections lie in different classes, or completion fails/normal form differs.
new.hypothesis: Two words are congruent iff, for every symbol s, deleting all other symbols gives the same word s...s (equal symbol projections). The shortlex-completed system {yx -> xy : x < y} is finite and its normal forms are the sorted words.
new.methodology: For every alphabet/length slice, compute the exact congruence classes by union-find over single swap steps; compare the partition with the projection partition; run shortlex Knuth-Bendix completion and compare normal forms with sorted words.
new.question: In System A with the swap relations xy <-> yx, what distinguishes two words that cannot be transformed into each other?
new.title: Commutation congruence: classes, complete invariant and normal forms

assumptions: System A, alphabet {a}
exponents are meta-level names for unary numerals
relations with 1-3 equations and exponents <= 20
new.falsification: Any relation set where completion yields a different rule, the class count differs from M + P, or the bounded union-find partition of small exponents differs from the formula.
new.hypothesis: The congruence generated by relations a^{m_i} = a^{n_i} (m_i < n_i) is the monogenic congruence with index M = min m_i and period P = gcd(n_i - m_i): exactly M + P classes, a^x ~ a^y iff x = y or (x, y >= M and x = y mod P).
new.methodology: Two independent methods per relation set: (1) shortlex Knuth-Bendix completion, reading index/period from the completed single rule and counting irreducible words; (2) union-find over exponents 0..B with all shifted relations (B = 6 max n). Compare both with the formula.
new.question: What structures arise when words over a single symbol a are identified by finitely many relations a^m = a^n?
new.title: One-symbol congruences: index and period of finitely generated congruences

assumptions: System A over {a} and over {a,b} modulo commutation
finite window of images
new.falsification: Any failure of a semiring axiom, or commuting compositions for all two-symbol samples.
new.hypothesis: Endomorphisms of {a}* (substitutions a -> w) with pointwise juxtaposition (f+g)(u) = f(u)g(u) and composition form a commutative semiring isomorphic to (N, +, x) via f -> f(a). With two symbols modulo commutation, composition is no longer commutative.
new.methodology: Represent an endomorphism by the image of a (a word). Implement substitution and juxtaposition on strings only; check every semiring axiom on all images a^0..a^K; check the length map is a homomorphism. For {a,b}/commutation, sample substitutions and look for non-commuting compositions.
new.question: Is there a second operation on unary numerals that arises from transformations alone?
new.title: Endomorphisms of the one-symbol free monoid form the semiring of natural numbers

assumptions: System A over {a,b}
relations of length 3 and 4
words of length <= 11
new.falsification: A word of length >= |u| whose class is strictly smaller than its Parikh class.
new.hypothesis: H-C01-4 (inventor's conjecture, deliberately bold): for every relation u <-> v over {a,b} with u != v and equal symbol counts, the generated congruence coincides with Parikh equivalence on all words of length >= |u|.
new.methodology: For each relation (up to swapping sides) compute exact congruence classes of each length (length-preserving, so exact), and compare their number and content with Parikh classes.
new.question: If a relation u <-> v only rearranges symbols, does it eventually identify all words with the same symbol counts (on long enough words)?
new.title: Single Parikh-preserving relations versus the Parikh (counting) equivalence

assumptions: System A
alphabets of size 2 (k = 2..5, n <= 12) and 3 (k = 2..3, n <= 7)
exact classes (relations preserve length)
new.falsification: Any relation with an unbordered side whose class counts differ from the series.
new.hypothesis: H-C01-5: if |u| = |v| = k, u != v and u is unbordered (no proper prefix equals a suffix), then the number of classes of length-n words over a q-letter alphabet equals [x^n] 1/(1 - q x + x^k), i.e. the number of length-n words avoiding u.
new.methodology: Exhaustive over all unordered pairs {u, v} of distinct words of length k. Exact class counts by union-find; compare with the series coefficients; for relations whose sides are both bordered, record counts, the minimal linear recurrence fitted to them, and whether shortlex completion terminates.
new.question: Why do all length-3 relations give F(n+3)-1 classes and most length-4 relations give partial sums of tribonacci numbers? Which relations are exceptions?
new.title: Class counts modulo one relation u <-> v: the unbordered-side theorem and its exceptions

assumptions: System A; length-preserving single relations u != v
binary k = 2..6 (n <= 12, k = 6 restricted to 'hard' pairs), ternary k = 2..4 (n <= 7, k = 4 restricted to hard pairs)
new.falsification: Any relation whose exact class counts differ from the formula.
new.hypothesis: H-C01-7: with k = |u| = |v|, q = alphabet size and c(x) = 1 + sum over words b that are borders of both u and v of x^(k-|b|), the class counts are the coefficients of c(x) / (x^k + (1 - q x) c(x)) (= the number of length-n words avoiding any single word whose autocorrelation is c).
new.methodology: Exact class counts by union-find. 'Hard' pairs are those where neither border set contains the other (the case not covered by the proved containment theorem); for k <= 5 binary and k <= 3 ternary all pairs are tested.
new.question: Is the number of classes of length-n words modulo u <-> v determined by the common borders of u and v?
new.title: Common-border formula for one-relation class counts (test on old and new cases)

assumptions: Newman's lemma and the critical-pair lemma for string rewriting
Cayley-Hamilton bound on the order of DFA count recurrences
new.falsification: A verified convergent completion whose irreducible-word counts differ from the formula would refute H-C01-7 for that relation.
new.hypothesis: For most small relations some shortlex order (alphabet permutation, read left-to-right or right-to-left) yields a finite convergent completion; its irreducible words then give a rational count sequence that can be compared with the formula exactly.
new.methodology: For each relation and each of 2*q! shortlex orders: run bounded Knuth-Bendix; on success, independently re-verify convergence (rules decreasing, all critical pairs joinable, u and v have equal normal forms); build the Aho-Corasick DFA of the left-hand sides (s live states); compare s + k + 5 count terms with the formula (sufficient for equality of all terms); cross-check against brute-force class counts for n <= 8.
new.question: For which relations u <-> v can H-C01-7 be proved for ALL lengths n by a finite certificate?
new.title: Automatic proofs of the common-border class-count formula via finite completion

new.applications: Linear-time decision of equality modulo commutation; justifies introducing N in System C.
new.novelty_basis: Free commutative monoid on Sigma is N^Sigma (Parikh vectors, Parikh 1966); special case of Mazurkiewicz trace monoids (Cartier-Foata 1969).
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (commEq_iff_count, projection_is_unary); standard axioms only
new.statement:
Two words over a finite alphabet are congruent modulo the swap relations xy = yx iff every symbol occurs
equally often in both; the projection of a word onto a symbol s is the unary word s...s of that length.
new.title: Symbol counts are the complete invariant of the commutation congruence

new.novelty_basis: Index and period of monogenic semigroups (e.g. Howie 1995, Fundamentals of Semigroup Theory).
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (gen_iff, exactly_m_add_p_classes); standard axioms only
new.statement:
On one-symbol words, a^x ~ a^y modulo a^m = a^(m+p) (p >= 1) iff nf(x) = nf(y) with nf(x) = x for x < m and
m + ((x - m) mod p) otherwise; there are exactly m + p classes.
new.title: One symbol, one relation a^m = a^(m+p) gives exactly m+p classes (index m, period p)

new.novelty_basis: Standard description of finitely generated congruences on (N,+) / cyclic semigroups.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C01.md, Theorem 3); computationally corroborated on 6159 relation sets; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
The congruence on {a}* generated by a^(m_i) = a^(n_i) (m_i < n_i, i = 1..r) identifies a^x and a^y iff
x = y or (x, y >= M and P | x - y), where M = min m_i and P = gcd(n_i - m_i); it has M + P classes.
new.title: Several one-symbol relations have index min m_i and period gcd(n_i - m_i)

new.novelty_basis: Endomorphism semiring of (N,+) is (N,+,x); endomorphisms of N^2 are 2x2 matrices over N.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C01.md, Theorem 4) with exhaustive check of all laws on a^0..a^12 (EXP-C01-03); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
(End({a}*), pointwise juxtaposition, composition) is a commutative semiring isomorphic to (N, +, x) via
phi -> |phi(a)|. For two symbols modulo commutation, composition of endomorphisms is not commutative.
new.title: Multiplication emerges as composition of substitutions; with two symbols it is non-commutative

new.counterexample: u = aab, v = aba: the word baa is fixed by every rewrite, so its class {baa} is smaller than its counting class {aab, aba, baa}. All 33 relations of length 3-4 fail (EXP-C01-04).
new.statement:
For every relation u <-> v over {a,b} with u != v and equal symbol counts, the generated congruence
coincides with counting (Parikh) equivalence on all words of length >= |u|.
new.title: H-C01-4: a single rearranging relation generates counting equivalence on long words (refuted)

new.applications: Exact information content of words modulo an invisible local rewrite (e.g. log2(phi) bits/symbol modulo aab = aba).
new.novelty_basis: Combination of Newman's lemma, the critical-pair lemma and Guibas-Odlyzko (1981); analogue of a one-element Groebner basis (Bergman 1978). Probably folklore; pending Historian audit.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C01.md, Theorem 5); its overlap lemma is Lean-verified (common_border_joinable); corroborated by 756 + 1632 relations; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
Let u != v be words of length k over a q-letter alphabet with Borders(u) contained in Borders(v). Then
{u -> v} is convergent, the classes of length-n words modulo u = v correspond to the length-n words
avoiding u, and the class-count generating function is c_u(x) / (x^k + (1 - q x) c_u(x)), c_u the
autocorrelation polynomial of u. For unbordered u this is 1/(1 - q x + x^k); for q = 2 the counts are
partial sums of (k-1)-bonacci numbers (k = 3: F(n+3) - 1).
new.title: Border-containment theorem for one length-preserving relation

new.proof_check: computer-assisted (Python) - independently re-verified convergent completion, Aho-Corasick automaton, recurrence-order bound s+k; brute-force cross-check n <= 8; not Lean-checked
new.statement:
For each of the 1632 relations marked PROVEN in results/EXP-C01-07.json (binary k <= 6, ternary k <= 4),
the class-count generating function equals c(x)/(x^k + (1 - q x) c(x)), c the common-border polynomial.
new.title: Common-border formula proved for 1632 specific relations by verified finite completions

new.limitations: Proved only in the border-containment case and for 1632 individual relations; 527 small relations remain open (infinite completions).
new.novelty_basis: Two web searches (2026-10-18) found no general formula; related literature - Nyberg-Brodda survey of one-relation monoids (arXiv:2105.02853), "Relations on words" (arXiv:1602.03364), Kudryavtseva 2010. Needs a deeper search (Hilbert series of one-relator algebras - Anick, Piontkovski, Iyudu).
new.statement:
For all words u != v of equal length k over a q-letter alphabet, the number of congruence classes of
length-n words modulo u = v has generating function c(x) / (x^k + (1 - q x) c(x)), where
c(x) = 1 + sum over words b that are borders of both u and v of x^(k - |b|).
new.title: Common-border conjecture: one-relation class counts depend only on common borders

new: Exact partitions of 25 slices coincide with symbol-count partitions; completion of the swap relations is the finite system {yx -> xy | x < y} whose normal forms are sorted words.
All 6159 relation sets agree with index = min m_i and period = gcd(n_i - m_i) under two independent methods.
Substitutions on one symbol form (N, +, x); on two symbols modulo commutation composition is non-commutative (154/200 random pairs).

Every one of the 33 rearranging relations of length 3-4 has words whose class is strictly smaller than their counting class; H-C01-4 refuted. Unexpected regularity in the class counts (Fibonacci and tribonacci partial sums) triggered H-C01-5.
aab <-> aba: class of baa is {baa}, counting class {aab, aba, baa}
H-C01-5 holds for all 756 relations with an unbordered side; 81 of the 281 relations with both sides bordered deviate from the generic count, all sharing a common border.
The common-border formula (H-C01-7) holds for all 2159 relations tested, including 1326 hard relations not covered by Theorem 5.
1632 relations proved for all n by independently re-verified finite completions; 527 hard relations have infinite completions within the search bounds.
Parametric (regular) completions for the 527 open relations

assumptions: configurations = multisets of levels (C01)
new.falsification: Two different normal forms, unequal derivation lengths, a cycle, or a mismatch with base-b digits.
new.hypothesis: Every derivation terminates in the same configuration, namely the base-b digits of n, after exactly (n - s_b(n))/(b - 1) exchanges, s_b the base-b digit sum.
new.methodology: Exhaustive derivation graphs from n tokens (all orders of exchange) for small n; fast stabilisation compared with base-b digits for n <= 20000.
new.question: Starting from n tokens at level 0 (a unary numeral), what does the exchange rule b[k] -> [k+1] produce, and does the order of exchanges matter?
new.title: Integer bases as normal forms of the exchange rule b tokens -> 1 token one level up

assumptions: weights w_k = F(k+2)
unary starts n <= 40; all configurations of value <= 26
new.falsification: A cycle, two sinks, or a sink different from the greedy Zeckendorf representation.
new.hypothesis: H-C02-F: from every configuration the system terminates and reaches a unique normal form, the Zeckendorf representation of its value (weights 1,2,3,5,8,...); unlike the binary rule, derivation lengths depend on the order of exchanges.
new.methodology: Exhaustive derivation graphs (cycle detection, sinks, min/max lengths) from unary starts and from every configuration of small value.
new.question: With exchanges [k]+[k+1] -> [k+2], 2[k] -> [k+1]+[k-2] (and boundary versions), do all orders of exchange reach the Zeckendorf representation, and how long do they take?
new.title: Fibonacci exchange rules: termination, confluence and derivation lengths

assumptions: m in {2,3,4}, b_j in {0..3}, J <= 3 (last coefficient nonzero): 189 rules
unary starts n <= 200; representations for n <= 3000
new.falsification: A rule with sum b < m and an infinite derivation, a rule with sum b >= m terminating from all n <= 200 with no glider, or a radix-order inversion.
new.hypothesis: H-C02-1: the rule terminates from every unary start iff sum_j b_j < m (emergent base r > 1, r the positive root of sum_j b_j r^j = m); otherwise some start produces a periodic glider. H-C02-2: for terminating rules, n < n' implies rep(n) < rep(n') in radix order.
new.methodology: Batch-firing upward sweep. After level k is processed the future depends only on the window (c_{k+1}, ..., c_{k+J}); a repeated nonzero window is a certificate of an infinite derivation (periodic glider). Radix order = compare length, then digits from the top.
new.question: Which carry rules turn unary numerals into finite normal forms, what is the emergent base, and are the resulting representations ordered like ordinary numerals?
new.title: Carry-rule survey: termination criterion, glider certificates and emergent bases

new: Batch-firing upward sweep. After level k is processed the future depends only on the window (c_{k+1}, ..., c_{k+J}), and the window map is monotone; a window W with an entry >= m that is later dominated componentwise (periodic glider if equal) certifies infinitely many firings. Radix order = compare length, then digits from the top.
old: Batch-firing upward sweep. After level k is processed the future depends only on the window (c_{k+1}, ..., c_{k+J}); a repeated nonzero window is a certificate of an infinite derivation (periodic glider). Radix order = compare length, then digits from the top.

assumptions: the 31 terminating rules of EXP-C02-03
exact arithmetic in Q(r) modulo the minimal polynomial of r
all stable configurations with at most L levels (m^L <= 2e5)
new.falsification: Two stable configurations with the same integer value; a merged sum that stabilises to something other than rep(a+b).
new.hypothesis: H-C02-4: for every terminating carry rule (sum b < m), distinct stable configurations of length <= L have distinct values, so each integer has exactly one stable representation. H-C02-5: stab(rep(a) + rep(b)) = rep(a + b).
new.methodology: Enumerate every stable configuration up to L levels, reduce sum c_k x^k modulo the minimal polynomial of r, keep those whose value is an integer, group by value. Addition: 2000 random pairs per rule.
new.question: In a terminating carry system, can an integer have a stable representation other than the normal form of its unary numeral? Does merging two normal forms and stabilising add them?
new.title: Uniqueness of stable representations in emergent bases; addition by merging

assumptions: the 31 terminating rules
all stable configurations supported on gZ with at most L supported levels (m^L <= 2e5)
new.falsification: A collision for a primitive irreducible P~, or no collision for a non-primitive P~.
new.hypothesis: H-C02-4': let g = gcd{j : b_j > 0} and P~(y) = sum_i b_(gi) y^i - m. If P~ is primitive and irreducible over Q, distinct stable configurations supported on multiples of g have distinct values; if P~ is not primitive, two such configurations with equal value exist.
new.methodology: Exact integer evaluation modulo the minimal polynomial (as in EXP-C02-04) restricted to levels 0, g, 2g, ...; compare collisions with the primitive/irreducible prediction.
new.question: Exactly which terminating carry rules have unique stable representations?
new.title: Refined uniqueness: primitive irreducible carry polynomials on the reachable sublattice

absence of a match is weak evidence of novelty only

new.novelty_basis: Chip-firing on a path / standard carrying.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C02.md Theorem 2) + exhaustive check of 134 derivation graphs and n <= 20000; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
From n tokens at level 0, every maximal derivation of the rule "b tokens at level k -> 1 token at level k+1"
(b >= 2) is finite, ends at the base-b expansion of n, and has exactly (n - s_b(n))/(b - 1) steps.
new.title: Integer bases emerge as normal forms of the exchange rule b[k] -> [k+1]

new.novelty_basis: Strong convergence of chip-firing (Bjorner-Lovasz-Shor 1991); abelian sandpile (Dhar 1990); abelian networks (Bond-Levine).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C02.md Theorem 1); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
For a carry rule m[k] -> sum_j b_j [k+j], one-step firings at different levels commute. Hence from any
configuration either all maximal derivations are infinite or all are finite with the same endpoint,
length and firing vector.
new.title: Abelian property of carry rules (order of exchanges is irrelevant)

new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C02.md Theorem 3); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
If sum_j b_j < m every derivation from every configuration terminates. If sum_j b_j > m, the emergent base
satisfies r < 1 and no derivation from n tokens at level 0 terminates when n > (m - 1)/(1 - r).
new.title: Termination dichotomy for carry rules away from sum b = m

new.limitations: Holds for all 28 surveyed rules (m <= 4, J <= 3, b_j <= 3); the general spreading step is unproved.
new.statement:
For every carry rule with sum_j b_j = m there is a unary start n whose sweep reaches a window dominating the
uniform-firing glider T = (T_1, ..., T_J), T_i = sum_{j >= i} b_j (or its g-sparse analogue, g the gcd of
the support of b); consequently its derivations from n are infinite. (Proved: T is a fixed point of the
window map and any window dominating T forces infinitely many firings.)
new.title: Carry rules with sum b = m never terminate from all unary starts (uniform glider)

new.proof_check: computer-assisted (Python) - explicit periodic-glider or monotone-pumping certificates for 158 rules; Theorem 3(a) for the 31 others
new.statement:
Among the 189 carry rules with m in {2,3,4}, J <= 3, b_j <= 3, exactly the 31 with sum b < m terminate from
every unary start; each of the other 158 has a unary start n <= 200 with an infinite derivation.
new.title: Termination classification for all 189 small carry rules (computer-assisted)

new.counterexample: 4[k] -> 2[k+1] (base 2 with digits 0..3): the stable configurations '2' and '10' both have value 2. Also 4[k] -> [k+2] on all levels, 4[k] -> 2[k+2], 4[k] -> 2[k+3] (EXP-C02-04).
new.statement: For every carry rule with sum b < m, each integer has exactly one stable configuration of that value.
new.title: H-C02-4: every terminating carry rule gives unique stable representations (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Gauss-lemma uniqueness arguments are classical for canonical number systems and generalized radix representations (Kovacs, Petho; Akiyama et al.); generalises the uniqueness of rational-base representations (Akiyama-Frougny-Sakarovitch 2008). Probably known; pending Historian audit.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the polynomial core (digits_unique, exists_large_coeff; standard axioms only); reduction to the lattice and the converse by written proof
new.statement:
Let g = gcd{j : b_j > 0} and P~(y) = sum_i b_(gi) y^i - m. If P~ is primitive and irreducible over Q, then
distinct stable configurations supported on multiples of g have distinct values; in particular every n has
exactly one stable representation there, namely rep(n). If P~ is not primitive, two such configurations with
equal value exist.
new.title: Uniqueness of representations when the reduced carry polynomial is primitive and irreducible

new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C02.md Theorem 6); 0 inversions for 31 rules up to n = 3000; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: For every carry rule with sum b < m and every n, rep(n) < rep(n+1) in radix order.
new.title: Exchange representations respect the radix order

new.novelty_basis: The Zeckendorf game (Baird-Smith, Epstein, Flint, Miller, arXiv:1809.04881) - termination and shortest game N - Z(N); OEIS A219641.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C02.md Theorem 8); exhaustive check of 2167 configurations; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
With weights 1,2,3,5,8,..., the exchanges [k]+[k+1] -> [k+2], 2[k] -> [k+1]+[k-2] (k >= 2), 2[1] -> [2]+[0],
2[0] -> [1] terminate from every configuration at the Zeckendorf representation of its value, and the
shortest derivation from n tokens at level 0 has n - z(n) steps (z(n) = number of Zeckendorf terms).
new.title: The Fibonacci exchange system terminates at the Zeckendorf representation; shortest derivation n - z(n)

new: Binary..quinary carrying from unary numerals is order-independent; normal forms are base-b expansions and every complete derivation has (n - s_b(n))/(b - 1) exchanges.
The Fibonacci exchange system reaches the Zeckendorf representation from every tested configuration; derivation lengths vary between n - z(n) and a larger maximum.

Termination from unary starts holds exactly for the 31 rules with sum b < m; every one of the 158 other rules has a periodic-glider or monotone-pumping certificate; no radix-order inversion up to n = 3000.
H-C02-4 refuted - four terminating rules have integers with several stable representations; merge-and-stabilise addition always agrees with rep(a+b).
4[k] -> 2[k+1]: configurations 2 (two tokens at level 0) and 10 (one token at level 1) are both stable with value 2
Uniqueness holds for all 28 rules whose reduced carry polynomial is primitive and irreducible (over all stable configurations, not only integer-valued ones) and fails for the 3 non-primitive ones.

Base 3/2 = A024629 and shortest Fibonacci derivations = A219641 (rediscoveries); longest Fibonacci derivations and exotic-base representations have no OEIS match. The A089881 hit for representation lengths is a spurious shifted-window coincidence.

new.statement:
(N>=1, o) with Knuth's product is a commutative cancellative semigroup without identity. The map
nu(n) = n phi + n*, n* = floor((n+1)/phi), is an injective homomorphism into (Z[phi], x); a o b = ab + ab* + a*b.
nu(n) is a unit iff n is a Fibonacci number F_k (k >= 2), and F_j o F_k = F_(j+k).

interval is circle-irreducible, and these n have natural density exactly 1/phi^2 = 0.381966...

new.statement:
(a) Abstractly: if every local peak b <- a -> c is joinable by two derivations of equal length, then whenever
a reaches a normal form b in n steps, every derivation from a has at most n steps and every derivation from a
to a normal form has exactly n steps and ends in b. (b) For any rule l -> r over any alphabet with l
unbordered, two distinct one-step reducts of a word have a common one-step reduct; hence (a) applies.

new.notes: Length uniformity alone is strictly weaker than random descent - 126 bordered length-preserving rules with |l| = 4, 5 are length-uniform on words <= 10 but not confluent (e.g. aaaba -> baabb on aaabaaaba).

new.statement:
For every rule l -> r (l != r) over a finite alphabet there are Phi : words -> Z and delta != 0 with
Phi(v) = Phi(u) + delta for every step u -> v (Phi = length if |l| != |r|; otherwise
Phi(w) = sum of i^K over positions i carrying a suitable letter c, K the least exponent at which the power
sums of the c-positions of l and r differ). Consequently all derivations between two given words have the same
number of steps, and a terminating one-rule system is confluent iff it has random descent.
new.title: Every one-rule system has a constant-step potential; for terminating ones confluence is equivalent to random descent

new.statement:
For aab -> ba over {a,b}, the maximal derivation length over words of length n >= 1 is
D(n) = n - 1 - kappa(n) with kappa(n) = min{k >= 0 : 2^k + k >= n}; D stalls exactly at n = 2^k + k + 1, and
the generating function of D is not rational. The proof identifies the rule with the binary exchange system
2[k] -> [k+1] (cycle C02) with an inert top level.
new.title: The rule aab -> ba has derivational complexity D(n) = n - 1 - min{k : 2^k + k >= n} (non-rational)

A(n) = n - max{j >= 0 : 2^j + j <= n + 1}, and A(n) = D(n + 2) where D is the derivational complexity of the
one-rule system aab -> ba.
new.title: Identity: OEIS A247983 (truncation index of the series for log 2) equals D(n+2) for aab -> ba

H-C14-7: Cartesian-prime and strong-prime connected graphs are equinumerous in every order (forced by unique factorisation and the common count of connected graphs).
new.methodology: For each product: find the composite graphs of orders 4 and 6 among the atlas graphs, take the rest as primes, enumerate all prime factorisations (multisets for commutative products, sequences otherwise) of every order <= 15, classify the products up to isomorphism, and record classes with more than one factorisation; repeat inside the class of connected graphs; verify the classical 63-vertex Cartesian counterexample (K1+K2+Q2)(K1+Q3) = (K1+Q2+Q4)(K1+K2).
new.question: For each associative local product with two-sided unit K1, which graphs of order <= 15 are composite, how many primes are there of each order, and where does unique factorisation fail?
new.title: Prime factorisation census for the eight associative local products with unit K1 (orders <= 15)

assumptions: C3 implemented from the paper's construction; its decoder reads one bit past each codeword (input virtually followed by '1'), so C3 is compared as a uniquely decipherable code
exact length comparison for n <= 2e6 and count inequalities for L <= 300 (big integers)
sources and data sets exactly as in EXP-C11-03 and EXP-C11-04
new.falsification: C3 shorter than T_011 for some n > 8; a round-trip failure; C3 better than T_011 on Zipf 1.1, log-uniform or the bursty posting list.
new.hypothesis: H-C11-5: C3 has 2F_L - 2 codewords of length <= L (Fraenkel-Klein Prop. 5), so T_011 (F_(L+2) - L - 1) is never longer than C3 except for a few small n, cum_011/cum_C3 -> phi^2/2, and T_011 has the smaller expected length on the heavy-tailed sources.
new.methodology: Check the first 12 codewords against the list printed in the paper, the length counts against 2F_(r-2) and the construction, round trips of concatenated streams, length(n) == len(encode(n)); compare length functions exactly; expected lengths on 12 sources and 4 data sets.
new.question: Fraenkel and Klein (1996) already improved the Fibonacci code C1 with C3, a uniquely decipherable but non-prefix code that is also decoded by searching for the pattern 011. Does T_011 still improve on the strongest code of that family?
new.title: Fraenkel-Klein C3 as a baseline: counts, exact length comparison with T_011 and C1, benchmarks

new.novelty_basis: Published theorem - for every N there is a unique operation on {1..N} with p*1 = p+1 mod N and p*(q*1) = (p*q)*(p*1), and it is left-distributive iff N is a power of 2 (R. Laver 1992/1995; elementary proof in A. Drapal's survey; see P. Dehornoy, Braids and Self-Distributivity (2000), Ch. X; P. Dehornoy, 'Some aspects of the SD-world', arXiv:1711.09792; P. Biane, arXiv:1810.00548). Lean checks A_3 and the non-existence for N = 3 (laver3_left_distributive, no_anchored_ld_three); the general theorem is not re-proved by the lab.
new.statement:
An anchored left-distributive magma (x*0 = x+1 mod N, x(yz) = (xy)(xz)) of size N exists exactly for
N = 1, 2, 4, 8 among N <= 10 and is then unique (the Laver table A_n); Laver's recursion yields
left-distributive tables exactly at the powers of 2 up to N = 64 (verified to N = 256 exhaustively).
new.title: Left-distributivity with a successor anchor: the Laver tables (rediscovery)

new.novelty_basis: Elementary (the anchor is a right translation by a generator); folklore.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (anchored_assoc_unique; standard axioms only)
new.statement: If * on Z/N is associative and x*0 = x + 1 for all x, then x*y = x + y + 1; conversely this operation is associative and anchored. So every N has exactly one anchored associative magma (a cyclic group).
new.title: Anchored associativity forces x*y = x + y + 1, for every N

new.novelty_basis: Elementary; explains why the anchor singles out left- and not right-distributivity.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (anchored_rd_unique; standard axioms only); written proof proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 2
new.statement: If (xy)z = (xz)(yz) on Z/N and x*0 = x + 1, then x*y = x + 1 for all x, y; conversely this operation is right-distributive and anchored.
new.title: Anchored right-distributivity forces x*y = x + 1, for every N

new.counterexample: 21 other laws have restricted spectra (EXP-C06-03): (xy)z = x((yz)z) - odd N; (xy)z = x(y(zz)) - N = 1, 5 (and 11, 19, ... by Theorem 6 of proofs/paper/C06.md); x(yz) = ((zx)x)y - N = 1, 3; x(yz) = ((xx)y)z - N = 1, 2.
new.statement: Among the laws x(yz) = t and (xy)z = t with t a term of 3-4 leaves over exactly {x, y, z}, every law other than left-distributivity has anchored spectrum {1} or {1, ..., 6}.
new.title: H-C06-2: a restricted anchored spectrum is special to left-distributivity (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Elementary consequence of the fact that the centraliser of an N-cycle consists of its powers.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 4); counts 1, 2, 9, 64, 625 for N <= 5 (EXP-C06-02); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: If (xy)z = (xz)y on Z/N and x*0 = x + 1, then x*y = x + c(y) for a function c with c(0) = 1; conversely every such operation is right-permutable and anchored. Hence there are exactly N^(N-1) anchored right-permutable magmas of size N.
new.title: Anchored right-permutable magmas are x*y = x + c(y); there are N^(N-1) of them

new.novelty_basis: Searches for anchored/successor-anchored magmas (2026-10-18) found only the Laver-table literature; no statement for this law. Small result.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (odd_law_even_impossible, odd_law_formula, odd_law_model; standard axioms only); written proof proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 5
new.statement: An anchored magma of size N satisfying (xy)z = x((yz)z) exists iff N is odd, and then x*y = x + 1 + y/2 (the inverse of 2 modulo N).
new.title: An 'odd' law: (xy)z = x((yz)z) has an anchored model exactly for odd N, and it is unique

new.novelty_basis: The number theory is classical (quadratic reciprocity and Hensel; OEIS A089270 and A087781 describe the moduli for which x^2 = x + 1 is solvable and count the roots, https://oeis.org/A089270, https://oeis.org/A087781). The correspondence between this magma law and the golden congruence was not found in the searches made (anchored-magma searches return only Laver tables).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 6); model counts equal the root counts for every N <= 12 (EXP-C06-04); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
The anchored magmas of size N satisfying (xy)z = x(y(zz)) are exactly x*y = x + 1 + a*y (mod N) with
a^2 + a = 1 (mod N); distinct roots give distinct models. Hence the spectrum is the set of N = 5^e m with
e in {0, 1} and every prime factor of m congruent to +-1 mod 5 (OEIS A089270: 1, 5, 11, 19, 29, 31, 41, 55, ...)
and the number of models is the number of roots (OEIS A087781).
new.title: A 'golden' law: anchored models of (xy)z = x(y(zz)) correspond to roots of a^2 + a = 1 mod N

new.novelty_basis: Left-permutable groupoids are studied (e.g. Stanovsky's surveys; Weber 2009 on commutativity identities), and the argument is the regular-representation idea (Cayley); no statement about anchored left-permutable magmas or their enumeration was found in one search (2026-10-18). Likely folklore in spirit; small.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the structural core (centralizer_eq, comp_eq, id_eq, leftPerm_assoc, leftPerm_comm, leftPerm_one_mul, leftPerm_mul_one; standard axioms only); the inverse construction is immediate (written proof proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 7); counts agree for N <= 5 (EXP-C06-02)
new.statement:
On Z/N, a.b := (a - 1)*b and x*y := (x + 1).y are inverse bijections between anchored magmas satisfying
x(yz) = y(xz) and commutative monoid structures with identity 0. Hence the number of anchored left-permutable
magmas of size N is the number of labelled commutative monoids of order N with a fixed identity (OEIS A058156:
1, 2, 9, 94, 1486, ...).
new.title: Anchored left-permutable magmas are commutative monoids in disguise (counted by OEIS A058156)

new.counterexample: x(yz) = y(x(yz)), x(yz) = y(x(xz)), x(yz) = y(y(xz)) and x(yz) = (yx)(yz) have anchored models for every N <= 6 but no affine model for N > 1; x(yz) = y((yx)z) has a non-affine model at N = 2 (EXP-C06-04).
new.statement: For every law of EXP-C06-03 other than left-distributivity, the anchored spectrum for N <= 6 equals the set of N for which some affine table x*y = x + a*y + 1 satisfies the law.
new.title: H-C06-3: anchored spectra are affine spectra (refuted)

new.limitations: Complete SAT enumeration for N <= 9; for all but x(yz) = y((yx)z) every model found is affine, and the affine spectrum is provably the stated finite set for all N (the affine conditions are polynomial congruences in a). Open - excluding non-affine models for N >= 10.
new.statement:
The seven laws x(yz) = ((zx)x)y, x(yz) = ((zx)y)x, x(yz) = ((zy)x)x, (xy)z = y((zx)y), (xy)z = y((zy)x),
(xy)z = z((yx)z), (xy)z = z((yz)x) have anchored models exactly for N in {1, 3}; the ten laws x(yz) = y((yx)z),
x(yz) = ((xx)y)z, x(yz) = ((xx)z)y, x(yz) = ((xy)x)z, x(yz) = ((xy)y)z, x(yz) = ((xy)z)x, x(yz) = ((xy)z)y,
x(yz) = ((xz)x)y, x(yz) = ((xz)y)x, x(yz) = ((xz)y)y have anchored models exactly for N in {1, 2}.
new.title: Laws with finite anchored spectra {1, 2} and {1, 3}

new.limitations: No proof that all their models are affine; the arguments of Theorems 5-6 do not transfer directly because the z = 0 substitution produces 0*(yy) and 0*y terms.
new.statement: (xy)z = x(z(yy)) has the same anchored model counts as the golden law (xy)z = x(y(zz)), and (xy)z = x((zy)y) the same as the odd law (xy)z = x((yz)z), for N <= 9; their affine spectra coincide for N <= 40.
new.title: Mirror twins of the golden and odd laws

new: Laver's recursion produces a left-distributive table exactly for N in {1, 2, 4, ..., 64} among N <= 64; the tables A_n are left-distributive for n <= 12 (exhaustively up to N = 256, 2e5 random triples beyond); the row-0 periods 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16, ... match OEIS A098820.

Complete SAT enumeration of successor-anchored models (x*0 = x+1 mod N) for 12 laws. Left-distributivity - exactly one model for N = 1, 2, 4, 8 and none for the other N <= 10 (H-C06-1 confirmed, independently of Laver's recursion). Right-distributivity, associativity, (xy)z = (xy)(xz) and x(yx) = xy - exactly one model for every N. Right-permutable - 1, 2, 9, 64, 625 = N^(N-1). Left-permutable - 1, 2, 9, 94, 1486 (OEIS A058156, commutative monoids with fixed identity). x(xy) = xy - 1, 2, 24, >= 2000. Four laws only N = 1. The first run was stopped and fixed - an unused isomorphism reduction (8! permutations per table) made it run for 30 minutes; anchored structures have no non-trivial anchored isomorphisms, so tables are counted directly.

All 382 laws x(yz) = t or (xy)z = t with t a term of 3-4 leaves using exactly x, y, z - 77 have anchored models for every N <= 6, 283 only for N = 1, and 22 have a restricted spectrum. Only one of the 22 is left-distributivity, so the bold hypothesis H-C06-2 is refuted. The restricted spectra (extended to N = 8) are {1,2} (10 laws), {1,3} (7 laws), {1,5} (2 laws), the odd numbers {1,3,5,7} (2 laws) and {1,2,4,8} (LD). No UNKNOWN instance.
(xy)z = x((yz)z): anchored models exactly for N = 1, 3, 5, 7 (N <= 8)
(xy)z = x(y(zz)): anchored models exactly for N = 1, 5 (N <= 8)
x(yz) = ((zx)x)y: anchored models exactly for N = 1, 3 (N <= 8)

Affine anchored models x*y = x + a*y + 1 explain 20 of the 22 restricted spectra - all their models for N <= 9 are affine - but not all spectra - 6 laws (LD, x(yz) = y((yx)z) and four laws with models for every N, e.g. x(yz) = y(x(yz))) have non-affine models, refuting H-C06-3. The hand-derived predictions hold exactly - (xy)z = x(y(zz)) has 1, 1, 2 models at N = 1, 5, 11 and none for other N <= 12 (roots of a^2 + a = 1 mod N); (xy)z = x((yz)z) has exactly one model for odd N <= 11 and none for even N.
x(yz) = y(x(yz)) has anchored models for every N <= 6 but no affine one for N > 1
x(yz) = y((yx)z) has a non-affine anchored model at N = 2

new.novelty_basis: Standard product construction (varieties are closed under direct products); the anchored reformulation answers the lab's question whether a spectrum can be the primes.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C06.md Theorem 8); consistent with every spectrum observed in EXP-C06-02..04; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: For every set of laws, if anchored models of coprime sizes N and M exist, then an anchored model of size NM exists (transport the direct product along the Chinese remainder isomorphism, which maps x + 1 to (x + 1, x + 1)). In particular no law has the set of primes as its anchored spectrum.
new.title: Anchored spectra are closed under coprime products

assumptions: switching classes of order n <= 8 obtained from all graphs with <= 7 vertices (order 8: a 7-vertex graph plus an isolated vertex represents every class)
switching equivalence decided exactly: same Seidel spectrum, then isomorphism of descendants
class counts validated against OEIS A002854
new.falsification: Two different multisets of prime two-graphs with switching-equivalent XOR products.
new.hypothesis: H-C14-4 (bold): every two-graph of order <= 16 has exactly one factorisation into prime two-graphs under XOR. H-C14-8: K2 xor X and K2 xor Y are isomorphic graphs iff X and Y are switching equivalent (the 'if' part is proved in Theorem 7; 'only if' is tested here for orders <= 7).
new.methodology: Classify switching classes by order, find composite classes (orders 4, 6, 8), enumerate all multisets of prime classes with product order n in {4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15,16}, classify the XOR products up to switching, record collisions; count primes per order.
new.question: The symmetric difference (XOR) product respects Seidel switching (Theorem 6). On switching classes (two-graphs), is factorisation into primes unique?
new.title: Prime factorisation of two-graphs under the symmetric-difference product

new.novelty_basis: Generating function: Guibas and Odlyzko (1981), string overlaps. Fibonacci code and its order-k generalisation: Apostolico and Fraenkel (1987), Fraenkel and Klein (1996); the 'N consecutive ones' generalisation is standard.
new.proof_check: Prefix property and unique parsing machine-checked in Lean (Infinity.C11.prefix_free, unique_parse_head; #print axioms: none); generating function and completeness by the written proof; implementations checked in EXP-C11-01 (Kraft partial sums >= 0.999999999993, C1 == T_11 for n <= 2e5)
new.statement:
For a binary pattern p of length k, the set T_p of binary words in which p occurs for the first time at the end
is a prefix code with Kraft sum 1, the number of its codewords of each length has generating function
x^k / (x^k + (1 - 2x) c_p(x)) with c_p the autocorrelation polynomial of p, and T_11 (T_(1^k)) is exactly the
codeword set of the Fibonacci code C1 (of its order-k generalisation).
new.title: Pattern-terminated codes T_p are complete prefix codes with counts x^k / (x^k + (1-2x) c_p(x)); T_11 is the Fibonacci code

new.novelty_basis: In substance the Guibas-Odlyzko comparison of patterns through their correlation polynomials (words avoiding a more self-overlapping pattern are more numerous); the codes share the avoidance denominator.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C11.md Theorem 2, from D_(1^k) - D_p = (1-2x)(c_(1^k) - c_p)); 0 violations among all 2044 patterns of length 2..10 (EXP-C11-02)
new.statement:
Let lambda_p = 1/rho_p, with rho_p the smallest positive root of x^k + (1 - 2x) c_p(x). Among binary patterns of
length k, 1^k and 0^k have the largest lambda_p and every other pattern has a strictly smaller one; hence
T_(1^k) has the smallest asymptotic codeword length log2(n)/log2(lambda) among length-k terminators.
new.title: The all-ones terminator 1^k (and 0^k) uniquely maximises the growth rate among length-k patterns

new.novelty_basis: An elementary consequence of the Guibas-Odlyzko generating function; the resulting count sequences are catalogued as partial sums (OEIS A000071 = Fibonacci(n) - 1, A008937 = partial sums of tribonacci numbers).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C11.md Theorem 3); 0 mismatches with exact integers for all unbordered patterns of length 3..9 up to length 200 (EXP-C11-06); ratios 1.618033989, 1.191487884, 1.078095078 for k = 2, 3, 4 (EXP-C11-02)
new.statement:
If u is unbordered and |u| = k + 1, the codeword counts of T_u are the partial sums of those of T_(1^k):
f_u(L) = cum_(1^k)(L - 1). Hence lambda_u is the k-bonacci constant lambda and cum_u(L)/cum_(1^k)(L) -> 1/(lambda - 1).
new.title: Unbordered terminators: F_u = x/(1-x) F_(1^k), so codeword counts are partial sums of the all-ones counts

new.applications: A drop-in prefix-free replacement for the Fibonacci code that saves one bit on almost every integer.
new.novelty_basis: Low confidence. Not found in Apostolico-Fraenkel (1987), Fraenkel-Klein (1996), Anisimov-Zavadskyi multi-delimiter codes (IEEE Trans. IT 63, 2017), the prefix-synchronised-code literature (Gilbert 1960; Guibas-Odlyzko 1978) or the standard accounts of Fibonacci coding. Closest prior art: Fraenkel-Klein's C3, a non-prefix improvement of C1 that is also decoded by searching for 011 (compared in CLM-C11-09).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C11.md Corollary 4); exhaustive check for n <= 2e6 (difference -1 at 3 values, 0 at 429, +1 at 1999568) and block-wise check up to L = 90 (EXP-C11-06)
new.statement:
cum_11(L) = F_(L+1) - 1 and cum_011(L) = F_(L+2) - L - 1. If the Fibonacci (C1) codeword of n has length L + 1,
the T_011 codeword is one bit shorter when n <= F_(L+2) - L - 1 and of equal length for the last L values of the
level; T_011 is longer than C1 only for n in {1, 2, 4}. The same holds for every unbordered 3-letter terminator.
new.title: T_011 is never longer than the Fibonacci code for n >= 5 and one bit shorter on all but L values per level

new.counterexample: k = 4, n = 1000: terminators 1000, 1001 and 1010 give codewords 1 bit shorter than 1111. Rivals beat 1^k at 762, 972 and 1127 sampled n >= 1000 (all n <= 2048 and quarter-powers of 2 up to 2^64) for k = 4, 5, 6, up to n = 311743, 2^45 and about 1.3e19 respectively (EXP-C11-02). By Theorem 2 (CLM-C11-02), 1^k does win eventually.
new.statement: For every k, the all-ones terminator 1^k gives the shortest codeword among all length-k terminators for every n beyond a small threshold.
new.title: H-C11-2: 1^k is the best length-k terminator beyond small n (refuted at practical sizes)

new.counterexample: k = 3 (111 vs 0111): the average over n <= 2^40 is 0.2282 against the prediction 0.2875 of (a) (EXP-C11-06); the running average is 0.228181, 0.309709 and 0.228548 at N = 2^40, 2^80 and 2^120, so it does not converge (EXP-C11-07). Both statements hold only for k = 2 (value 1).
new.statement:
(a) The average over n <= N of L_(1^k)(n) - L_u(n), u unbordered of length k + 1, tends to log_lambda(1/(lambda - 1)).
(b) Corrected version: this average converges to (2 - lambda)/(lambda - 1)^2.
new.title: Average gain of an unbordered terminator over 1^k: log_lambda(1/(lambda-1)), then convergence to (2-lambda)/(lambda-1)^2 (both refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Low confidence. Log-periodic oscillation of averages is a generic phenomenon in the analysis of algorithms; the specific constants for pattern-terminated codes were not found in the sources listed for CLM-C11-04.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C11.md Proposition 5); both constants agree to 6 digits with exact averages at L = 100, 200, 400 for k = 2..6 (EXP-C11-08)
new.statement:
For k >= 2, lambda the k-bonacci constant and u unbordered of length k + 1, the running average
G(N) = (1/N) sum_(n<=N) (L_(1^k)(n) - L_u(n)) has liminf (2 - lambda)/(lambda - 1)^2 and limsup
lambda(2 - lambda)/(lambda - 1) (both 1 for k = 2; 0.228155 and 0.352201 for k = 3).
new.title: The average gain oscillates between (2-lambda)/(lambda-1)^2 and lambda(2-lambda)/(lambda-1)

new.applications: Universal coding of heavy-tailed integer streams of unknown scale (posting-list gaps, magnitudes spread over many orders).
new.limitations: 12 synthetic sources (exact expectations) and 4 data sets, two of them simulated; memoryless codes compared with zeroth-order entropy; tuned codes are tuned on the evaluated data (optimistic for them); CPython string implementations without table-driven decoding; no claim of optimality beyond the tested baselines.
new.statement:
Among fixed (untuned) universal codes, a pattern-terminated code (T_101, T_0111 or T_00111) has the smallest
expected length on 5 of 12 synthetic sources (Zipf 1.1, geometric 0.001, uniform 2^16, uniform 2^32,
log-uniform on [1, 1e6]) and on both posting-list data sets, beating the best classical universal code
(Elias, Levenshtein, Fibonacci, Fraenkel-Klein C3, LEB128, fixed Exp-Golomb) by 0.34-3.06 bits per value; on
Zipf 1.1, log-uniform and the bursty posting list it also beats Golomb and Exp-Golomb codes tuned to the source.
It loses on light-tailed sources (Zipf >= 1.5, geometric >= 0.01, prime gaps) and to tuned Golomb/Exp-Golomb
codes on geometric and uniform sources, and the reference implementation is 4-10 times slower than the Elias
and Exp-Golomb codes.
new.title: Fixed pattern-terminated codes beat classical universal codes on heavy-tailed and wide-range sources (mixed result)

new.novelty_basis: Low confidence. The count 2F_(r-2) and the comparison C3 <= C1 (for n > 1) are Fraenkel and Klein's (Discrete Appl. Math. 64, 1996, Propositions 5-6); the comparison with T_011 is new only insofar as T_011 itself is (CLM-C11-04).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C11.md Corollary 6, from cum_011(L) - cum_C3(L) = F_(L-1) - (L - 1)); exhaustive check for n <= 2e6 and the count inequalities for L < 300 (EXP-C11-09)
new.statement:
The Fraenkel-Klein code C3 (2F_(r-2) codewords of length r >= 3, so cum_C3(L) = 2F_L - 2) is never longer than the
Fibonacci code C1 except at n = 1, and T_011 is never longer than C3 except at n in {2, 4, 8}; moreover
cum_011(L)/cum_C3(L) -> phi^2/2 and cum_C3(L)/cum_C1(L) -> 2/phi.
new.title: T_011 is never longer than Fraenkel-Klein's C3 except at n = 2, 4, 8; C3 is never longer than C1 except at n = 1

new:
All 78 implementations (9 baseline universal codes, 61 pattern-terminated codes, 8 Golomb/Rice codes) round-trip,
are prefix-free on their first 20000 codewords and have nondecreasing length functions; Kraft partial sums of the
pattern codes lie in [0.999999999993, 1] at lengths <= 1500; Fibonacci C1 and T_11 have the same length function
for n <= 2e5. The first runs failed on test-design errors (a table too short for growth-rate-1 patterns, a
monotonicity check on an unsorted list giving 70 false problems, Kraft sums of 0.865 at lengths <= 120); they
stay in the run history.

1^k and 0^k uniquely maximise the growth rate for every k = 2..10 (2044 patterns, 0 violations); unbordered
patterns have the (k-1)-bonacci growth rate (0 violations); roots and count ratios agree to 1.3e-15. But rival
terminators beat 1^k at 762 / 972 / 1127 sampled n >= 1000 for k = 4 / 5 / 6, the last up to n = 1.3e19.
Count sequences of 011, 101, 0101, 0111, 0110/1011 are OEIS A000071, A005314, A112575, A008937, A059633.
H-C11-2: k = 4, n = 1000: terminators 1000, 1001, 1010 give codewords 1 bit shorter than 1111.

Exact expected lengths on 12 sources. A fixed pattern code is the best fixed universal code on Zipf 1.1 (T_101,
redundancy 0.1935), geometric 0.001 (T_0111, 1.735), uniform 2^16 (T_0111, 3.2978), uniform 2^32 (T_00111,
4.4391) and log-uniform (T_0111, 0.4006); classical codes win on the other 7 (Zipf >= 1.5, geometric >= 0.01,
uniform 2^8). Tuned Golomb codes are nearly optimal on geometric sources (redundancy <= 0.0352) and best on
uniform ones (0.5), but poor on Zipf 1.1 (5.3783) and log-uniform (3.9299).

Prime gaps <= 1e7: Exp-Golomb (raw 5.7208, halved 4.5787 bits) is the best fixed code and tuned Golomb the best
overall (5.2713, 4.2713). Posting lists: T_0111 is the best fixed code on geometric gaps (13.1548, tuned Golomb
11.446) and T_101 the best code overall on the bursty mixture (11.4728 vs Fibonacci 12.1459, tuned Exp-Golomb
11.7868, tuned Golomb 12.8038).

All 14 implementations round-trip on 1e5 log-uniform values below 2^20; bits per value T_0111 14.20, T_111
14.31, T_101 14.41, Fibonacci 15.57, Elias delta 15.89. The string-based pattern codes need about 3 us per value
against 0.4-0.7 us for the Elias codes and 2.1 us for Fibonacci (CPython; machine-dependent, outside the result
hash).

F_u = x/(1-x) F_(1^k) holds with 0 mismatches for all unbordered u of length 3..9 up to length 200. T_011 is
longer than Fibonacci only for n in {1, 2, 4}; for n <= 2e6 the difference (Fibonacci - T_011) is -1 three times,
0 429 times and 1 1999568 times; block checks up to L = 90 find no violation. The predicted average gain
log_lambda(1/(lambda-1)) fails for k >= 3 (0.2282 measured vs 0.2875 for k = 3).
Average gain of 0111 over 111 for n <= 2^40: 0.2282, predicted 0.2875.

The corrected constant (2-lambda)/(lambda-1)^2 matches the running average at 2^40 and 2^120 for k = 3 (0.228181,
0.228548 vs 0.228155) but not at 2^80 (0.309709): the average gain does not converge for k >= 3.

At level ends the running average equals (2-lambda)/(lambda-1)^2 and at the ends of the saved segments
lambda(2-lambda)/(lambda-1), to 6 digits for k = 2..6 at L = 100, 200, 400 (k = 3: 0.228155 and 0.352201).

Fraenkel-Klein C3 implemented from the paper (first 12 codewords equal the printed list, 0 problems, Kraft
partial sum 1, not prefix-free). For n <= 2e6, C3 is longer than C1 only at n = 1 and T_011 longer than C3 only
at n in {2, 4, 8}; (C3 - T_011) is 1 bit for 1167558 values and 0 for 832439; the count inequalities fail only at
L = 3, 4, 5 (T_011 vs C3) and L = 2 (C3 vs C1) for L < 300; cum_011/cum_C3 = 1.309016994 = phi^2/2. The average
of L_C1 - L_C3 is 0.462, 0.400, 0.481 over n <= 2^40, 2^80, 2^120 (the T_011 gain over C1 is the complement to
1). C3 beats T_011 on Zipf 1.5/2/3, geometric 0.5/0.1 and both prime-gap data sets, and loses on the other 9.

new.novelty_basis:
Iannucci & Larsson, "Game values of arithmetic functions" (arXiv:2101.07608, 2021), Theorem 1 (maliquot =
G04) and Theorem 2 (saliquot = G02); G01 is the "Divisor Game" puzzle (LeetCode 1025) and its Grundy
function follows from the saliquot proof. OEIS A007814, A001511, A001222.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 1); 0 mismatches for n <= 1e5 (EXP-C12-02)
new.statement:
G01 (n -> n - d with d | n, d < n) has Grundy function g(n) = v2(n) (n >= 1); G02 (d = n also allowed) has
g(n) = v2(n) + 1 (n >= 1); G04 (n -> d with d | n, d < n) has g(n) = Omega(n).
new.title: Divisibility games: subtract a proper divisor = v2, subtract a divisor = v2 + 1, move to a divisor = Omega

new.limitations: The odd values of G06 have no closed form; g(m)/m < 0.24985 for odd m <= 5000 (a bound m/4 is not proved).
new.novelty_basis:
Iannucci & Larsson 2021, Theorem 5 (totative = G05, with the subtraction equivalence) and Theorem 6
(nontotative: SG(2n) = n, SG(n) = 1 iff n prime, i.e. our G06 values plus one; they also prove SG(n) <= n/2).
OEIS A055396, A279119 (= G06 exactly), A008578.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 2); 0 mismatches for n <= 5000 (G07 = G05 for n <= 1500) (EXP-C12-02)
new.statement:
G05 (n -> m, 1 <= m < n, gcd(m, n) = 1), which coincides with "subtract k, 1 <= k < n, gcd(k, n) = 1", has
g(1) = 0 and g(n) = j for n >= 2, where the smallest prime factor of n is the j-th prime. G06 (n -> m,
1 <= m < n, gcd(m, n) > 1) has g(2k) = k - 1, g(m) <= (m - 1)/2 for odd m, and its P-positions n >= 1 are
exactly 1 and the primes.
new.title: Coprimality games: index of the smallest prime factor; the non-coprime game has g(2k) = k - 1

new.novelty_basis:
Codeforces problem 1537D "Deleting Divisors" (Round #726, June 2021): the official solution declares the
second player the winner exactly for odd n and for n = 2^k with k odd. First assessed as potentially novel
(no OEIS match); downgraded after the Historian found the problem.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib: Infinity.C12.g03_pset and Infinity.C12.g03_P_positions (axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no sorry, no native_decide); 0 mismatches for n <= 1e5 (EXP-C12-02)
new.statement:
In G03 (n -> n - d with d | n and 1 < d < n) the P-positions are exactly 0, the odd numbers and the powers
2^(2j+1).
new.title: P-positions of the deleting-divisors game (subtract d | n with 1 < d < n): 0, odd numbers, 2^(2j+1)

new.applications: Sums of deleting-divisors heaps are solved by XOR of closed-form values (the P-positions alone do not solve sums).
new.limitations: The written inductive step awaits independent Skeptic review; beyond a = 100 the certificate relies on the shift-invariance argument.
new.novelty_basis:
The Grundy sequence is not in the OEIS (EXP-C12-04, queried 2026-10-18); the game is not among the divisor
games of Iannucci & Larsson 2021; Codeforces 1537D and its solution determine only the P-positions; web
searches (2026-10-18) found no analysis of the Grundy values. Not a priority claim.
new.proof_check:
Computer-assisted (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 8): exact computation for n <= 1e5 and an inductive-step
certificate for odd parts <= 15 and 13 <= a <= 100 (EXP-C12-06, 0 failures); written induction for odd parts
>= 17 and shift-invariance argument for odd parts <= 15; odd n via the Lean P-set theorem g03_pset. Trust
base: exact Python integer arithmetic plus the written Steps 2-3 (not yet reviewed by the Skeptic).
new.statement:
Let g be the Grundy function of G03 and n = 2^a m with m odd. Then g(n) = 0 for odd n, and for a >= 1:
g(2^a m) = a if m >= 17; g(2^a) = 0 for odd a and a - 1 for even a, except g(16) = 2; for m = 3 the values
are 2, 3, 4, 3, 6 (a = 1..5) and a - 2 (a >= 6); for m = 5 they are 1, 3, 4, 3, 6 (a = 1..5) and a + 2
(a >= 6); for m = 7, 9, 11, 15 they are a (a <= 2) and a + 1 (a >= 3); for m = 13 they are a (a <= 3) and
a + 1 (a >= 4). Consequently |g(n) - v2(n)| <= 2 unless n is an odd power of 2, and the record values occur
at n = 5 * 2^a for a >= 6.
new.title: Grundy function of the deleting-divisors game: v2(n) except on odd parts <= 15

new.novelty_basis:
G19 is the residue-throw-divisor game, Theorem 12 of Iannucci & Larsson 2021 (proof left to the reader there;
our written proof supplies it). Sequences OEIS A000120, A099396 (g(n) = A099396(n + 1)), A000523. G13 is Nim
on the number of 1-bits; the quotient game G20 was not located in the literature but its analysis is
elementary.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 4); 0 mismatches for n <= 1e5, 5000 and 2e4 respectively (EXP-C12-02)
new.statement:
G13 (move to a proper binary submask) has g(n) = popcount(n); G19 (n -> n mod k, 1 <= k < n) has
g(n) = floor(log2((n + 1)/3)) + 1 for n >= 2 (g(0) = g(1) = 0); G20 (n -> floor(n/k), 2 <= k <= n) has
g(n) = floor(log2 n) for n >= 1.
new.title: Bitwise and quotient games: popcount, floor(log2((n+1)/3)) + 1 and floor(log2 n)

new.proof_check: (a) machine-checked in Lean (Infinity.C12.residue_grundy, Infinity.C12.power_of_two_grundy; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no sorry); (b) written proof (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 5); 0 mismatches for k = 2..20, n <= 2e4 (EXP-C12-02)
new.statement:
(a) If no element of the move set S is divisible by q and 1, ..., q - 1 are in S, the subtraction game S has
g(n) = n mod q; in particular subtract-a-power-of-2 has g(n) = n mod 3. (b) For every k >= 2,
subtract-a-power-of-k has the same Grundy function as the subtraction game {1, k}: n mod 2 for odd k, and
P(n mod (k + 1)) with P(r) = r mod 2 for r < k and P(k) = 2 for even k.
new.title: Residue lemma; subtract-a-power-of-k has the Grundy function of the subtraction game {1, k}

new.novelty_basis: Classical parity argument (every move adds one heap, as in the chocolate-bar puzzle); the sequences are OEIS A000035 / A059841.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib: Infinity.C12.split_parity (axioms propext, Quot.sound; no sorry); G16, G17 and 40 random splitting relations checked (EXP-C12-02)
new.title: Splitting games in which every heap can be split have g(n) = [n even]

new.novelty_basis:
For squares the P-set is a maximal square-difference-free set, of density zero by Furstenberg-Sarkozy
(Wikipedia "Square-difference-free set"; D. Eppstein, "Faster evaluation of subtraction games", FUN 2018).
The triangular case is the same argument with an intersective polynomial.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C12.md Theorem 7) from the Furstenberg-Sarkozy theorem and its polynomial version (Kamae-Mendes France 1978), which are cited, not re-proved; P-densities 0.0222 and 0.0116 at n <= 2e5 (EXP-C12-03)
new.statement:
For the subtraction games whose move sets are the positive squares and the triangular numbers, the set of
P-positions is infinite and has natural density 0; hence neither Grundy sequence is eventually periodic or
eventually arithmetic-periodic.
new.title: Subtract-a-square and subtract-a-triangular-number have infinite density-zero P-sets and are not periodic

new.limitations: The "closed form" clause is not precisely defined, so the hypothesis cannot be refuted as stated; recorded as inconclusive rather than refuted.
new.notes:
13 of 19 games conform (5 periodic; closed forms for G01-G05, G13, G19, G20, G03 by CLM-C12-04).
Subtract-a-square and subtract-a-triangular-number are provably neither eventually periodic nor
arithmetic-periodic (CLM-C12-08), but the absence of a closed form is not a theorem. G06 (odd values),
subtract-a-Fibonacci, subtract-a-prime and Grundy's game remain unexplained within range (whether Grundy's
game is eventually periodic is a well-known open problem).
new.statement:
Every game of the catalogue is eventually periodic, eventually arithmetic-periodic, or has a Grundy function
given by a closed form in a number-theoretic function.
new.title: H-C12-0: every relational game is periodic, arithmetic-periodic or has a closed form (inconclusive)

new.counterexample:
G01: n = 2 and n = 3 have signature (1) but g = 1 and 0. Further first counterexamples: G02 (2, 3: g = 2, 1),
G03 (4, 9: 1, 0), G05 (2, 3: 1, 2), G06 (6, 10: 2, 4). Only G04 (g = Omega) depends on the signature alone.
new.statement: For each of the games G01-G06, g(n) depends only on the prime signature (sorted exponent vector) of n.
new.title: H-C12-1: Grundy values of divisibility/coprimality games depend only on the prime signature (refuted)

new.counterexample:
Squares and triangular numbers: the P-set has density 0 (CLM-C12-08); measured P-density 0.0538 -> 0.0222 and
0.0344 -> 0.0116 as N grows from 1.25e4 to 2e5. For Fibonacci numbers (0.180) and primes (0.155) the question
remains open.
new.statement:
Subtraction games whose move sets are the squares, the triangular numbers, the Fibonacci numbers or the primes
have P-positions of positive natural density.
new.title: H-C12-2: sparse move sets keep a positive density of P-positions (refuted)

new.limitations: Our own check covers n <= 2e5 only (maximum 11 from n <= 1.25e4 on).
new.novelty_basis:
OEIS A014589 records a(n) <= 11 for n <= 32452842 (A. Huet, 2022) and for n <= 1e9 (B. Dobbelaere, 2024);
we found no proof of boundedness.
new.statement: The Grundy values of the subtraction game whose move set is the set of primes satisfy g(n) <= 11 for all n.
new.title: Subtract-a-prime has Grundy values at most 11

new.limitations: Weak support - the maximum rose from 13 to 14 between n = 2.5e4 and 5e4 and is unchanged up to 2e5.
new.notes: The P-density is at most 1/5 by Pond and Howells (1965), as cited in OEIS A001581; measured 0.180 at n <= 2e5.
new.statement:
The Grundy values of the subtraction game with move set {1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...} (Fibonacci numbers) are bounded;
the observed maximum is 14 for n <= 2e5.
new.title: Subtract-a-Fibonacci-number has bounded Grundy values

new:
19 games: 5 eventually periodic (subtract a power of 2, 3, 4 with periods 3, 2, 5; coprime and dividing
splits with period 2), none arithmetic-periodic, 14 without either behaviour within range. The first run
reported spurious end-of-range periods; the detector now requires the periodic tail to cover half the range
and the census was re-run (both runs on record).

Every closed form matches the exact values with 0 mismatches (v2, v2 + 1, Omega, popcount up to 1e5; prime
index, G06 formulas, remainder game up to 5000; floor-division game up to 2e4; G03 P-positions up to 1e5;
powers of k for k = 2..20 up to 2e4; 40 random splitting relations up to 1500). Largest g(m)/m over odd
m <= 5000 in G06 is 0.24985.

P-density from N = 1.25e4 to 2e5: squares 0.0538 -> 0.0222 and triangular numbers 0.0344 -> 0.0116 (counts
growing roughly like N^0.67 and N^0.61), consistent with density zero; Fibonacci 0.169 -> 0.180 and primes
0.135 -> 0.155 do not decay. Maximal Grundy values grow for squares (36 -> 95) and triangular numbers
(50 -> 144) but stay at 14 (Fibonacci, from 5e4 on) and 11 (primes).

18 of 19 Grundy sequences are in the OEIS; the G10c hit (a shifted window of A014586) is spurious and G19 is
A099396 shifted by one index. Only G03 matches nothing, for both its Grundy and its P-position sequence.

H-C12-1 fails for G01, G02, G03, G05, G06 (first counterexamples (2, 3), (2, 3), (4, 9), (2, 3), (6, 10));
only G04 (g = Omega) depends on the prime signature alone.

The closed form of Theorem 8 equals the Grundy function of G03 on [0, 1e5]; the 96 positions with
g != v2 all have odd part <= 15; the inductive-step certificate (odd parts <= 15, 13 <= a <= 100) and 4000
random mex checks beyond the computed range have 0 failures.

assumptions: laws up to renaming of variables and exchange of sides; s != t
affine spectra computed through prime powers <= 200 (CRT); finite spectra computed exactly from a resultant bound
OEIS lookups of every infinite spectrum (terms <= 200)
new.falsification: A finite affine spectrum that is not the set of divisors of its maximum, or a spectrum that is not divisor-closed, would contradict the (proved) Theorem 1 of proofs/paper/C13.md and reveal an implementation error.
new.hypothesis: H-C13-3: affine spectra are exactly the sets {N : a fixed polynomial system has a root mod N}; they are divisor-closed and closed under coprime products, every finite one is the set of divisors of a single integer, and the infinite ones are governed by the Q-gcd of the system (a classical quadratic/cubic residue condition plus finitely many exceptional primes).
new.methodology: Evaluate both sides as linear forms with coefficients in Z[a]; the law's affine system is the set of coefficient differences. Group laws by system, then systems by spectrum. For each system compute the gcd over Q[a]; if it is constant, bound the spectrum by the gcd of the pairwise resultants R and find the largest prime powers dividing R that admit a common root; otherwise record the gcd polynomial. Look up every infinite spectrum in the OEIS and record the hits.
new.question: For every law s = t over {x,y,z} with at most 4 leaves per side (up to renaming and exchange of sides), and every law over {x,y} with at most 5 leaves per side, which sets of N admit an affine anchored model x*y = x + a*y + 1 (mod N)? Which arithmetic sets occur?
new.title: Atlas of affine anchored spectra for all laws with at most 4 leaves per side (and 2-variable laws with at most 5)

new.methodology: XOR: Seidel spectrum = {(s+1)(t+1) - 1}; strong: adjacency spectrum = {(a+1)(b+1) - 1}; co-normal: spectrum of J - A multiplies; Cartesian: adjacency spectrum = {a + b}. Compare sorted spectra and wall-clock times (median of 3).

new.title: Spectra of symmetric-difference, strong, co-normal and Cartesian products from the factors

symmetry breaking 0*0 in {0,1} (any magma can be relabelled so)
CaDiCaL conflict budget 1e6 per instance; UNKNOWN is reported as such

assumptions: rows a = 1..5 computed to b < 1500 for the first spec of each of the 134 distinct operations of EXP-C07-01; a row counts as additively periodic if a period p <= 375 holds on a checked tail of length >= max(200, 3p)

H-C07-5 (from inspection of EXP-C07-02): row 2 of D[x^y], g(b) = mex(G u (b XOR G)) with G = {g(b') : b' < b}, satisfies g(b) = b + J_k for J_(k+1) <= b < J_(k+1) + J_k and g(b) = b - J_k for J_(k+1) + J_k <= b < J_(k+2) (k >= 1), J the Jacobsthal numbers.

new.statement:
In the family of 512 mex operations (options f(a',b) [L], f(a,b') [R] and XOR combinations of f(a',b),
f(a,b'), f(a',b') [D]), the canonical specs empty, L, R, D[x], D[y], D[z], L+R, D[x^y^z], L+R+D[z],
D[x]+D[y], D[x]+D[y]+D[z] define for all a, b the operations 0, a, b, a[b>0], b[a>0], min(a,b), a XOR b,
a (x) b (nim-product), a + b, ((a-1) XOR (b-1)) + 1 and a + b - 1 (the last two with 0 absorbing), all
associative; 468 of the 512 specs are not associative; the remaining 33 specs agree with one of the 11
operations on [0,64)^2.
new.title: The associative mex operations are 0, projections, min, +, XOR, nim-product and four relatives

new.counterexample: L+R+D[z] gives ordinary addition a + b and D[z] gives min(a, b) (Theorem 1); also the zero-absorbing shifts of XOR and +.
new.statement: Apart from trivial operations (0, projections), the only associative mex operations of the family are Conway's nim-sum and nim-product.
new.title: H-C07-1: only nim-sum and nim-product are non-trivially associative (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Elementary.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C07.md Theorem 2, two-line induction); all 34 commutative operations of EXP-C07-02 conform
new.statement: If the spec contains L and R then f(0,b) = b and f(a,0) = a; if it contains neither, f(0,b) = f(a,0) = 0.
new.title: In a mex operation with both L and R options 0 is an identity; with neither, 0 is absorbing

new.counterexample: D[x^y]: f(2,3) = 4, so [0,4) is not closed; 30 of the 34 commutative operations fail (EXP-C07-01).
new.statement: Every commutative mex operation of the family is closed on [0, 2), [0, 4) and [0, 16), like the nimbers.
new.title: H-C07-2: commutative mex operations are closed on the Fermat segments [0, 2^(2^m)) (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: OEIS: no match for the row (2, 1, 4, 3, 8, 9, 10, 5, ...), for |g(b) - b| or for g(b) XOR b; text searches for greedy XOR-avoiding permutations found unrelated entries (A109812, A357578); a web search found no mex recursion of this form (closest: Multiplicative Modular Nim, arXiv:2507.08830, a different recursion). Small.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C07.md Theorem 3, induction over Jacobsthal blocks using J_(k+1) + J_k = 2^k and bit estimates); formula verified for all b < 2^15 by an independent bitset implementation (EXP-C07-03); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
For the mex operation D[x^y], f(a,b) = mex{f(a',b) XOR f(a,b') : a' < a, b' < b}: f(0,b) = 0, f(1,b) = b, and
g(b) = f(2,b) satisfies g(0) = 0 and, for every k >= 1, g(b) = b + J_k for 2^k - J_k <= b < 2^k and
g(b) = b - J_k for 2^k <= b < 2^k + J_k, where J_k = (2^k - (-1)^k)/3 are the Jacobsthal numbers. Equivalently,
g(b) is the least v with v and v XOR b both outside {g(b') : b' < b}. The row is an involution and is not
additively periodic.
new.title: The Jacobsthal row: row 2 of f(a,b) = mex{f(a',b) XOR f(a,b')} swaps the blocks [2^k - J_k, 2^k) and [2^k, 2^k + J_k)

new.counterexample: Row 2 of D[x^y] (Theorem 3): |f(2,b) - b| = J_k on the k-th block pair, which rules out every (p, s). Numerically only 222 of 670 rows (a = 1..5, b < 1500) have a period <= 375.
new.statement: For every operation of the family and every a, the row b -> f(a,b) satisfies f(a, b + p) = f(a, b) + s for all large b, for some p >= 1 and s, as for Wythoff's game.
new.title: H-C07-4: every row of every mex operation is eventually additively periodic (refuted)

new.counterexample: The first part holds (Theorem 2); the second fails - e.g. the diagonal 0, 2, 1, 5, 7, 4, 3, 16, 13, 10, 15, 6, ... of L+R+D[x^y^z] and 0, 1, 3, 6, 8, 11, 10, 19, ... of D[z]+D[x^y^z] have no OEIS match (88 unmatched sequences, EXP-C07-02, OEIS state of 2026-10-18).
new.statement: For every commutative mex operation of the family, 0 is absorbing or an identity, and the diagonal f(n,n) is a sequence in the OEIS.
new.title: H-C07-3: the diagonals of commutative mex operations are known sequences (refuted)

new.limitations: Finite windows; a row without a detected period may have a longer one.
new.statement: Among the 134 distinct mex operations, 22 have additively periodic rows a = 1..5 (period <= 375 within b < 1500), 40 have none, and the rest are mixed.
new.title: Additive periodicity is the exception among mex operations

new: The 512 specs give 134 distinct operations on [0,64)^2, 34 commutative. Exactly 11 operations (44 specs) show no associativity violation on the evaluable triples of [0,16)^3 and [0,64)^3; they are 0, a, b, a[b>0], b[a>0], min, a+b, XOR, nim-product and zero-absorbing shifts of XOR and +. The other 468 specs have explicit violating triples. 30 of the 34 commutative operations are not closed on [0,2), [0,4) or [0,16).
L+R+D[z] = a + b and D[z] = min(a, b) are associative (H-C07-1 refuted)
D[x^y]: f(2,3) = 4, so [0,4) is not closed (H-C07-2 refuted)

In all 34 commutative operations 0 is absorbing (no L, R options) or an identity (L and R); no simple closed form for the chaotic ones (tested candidates a^b^ab, (a^1)(b^1)^1, ab, ...). Of the diagonals and rows 1-3 looked up, 88 sequences have no OEIS match (e.g. the diagonal 0, 2, 1, 5, 7, 4, 3, 16, ... of L+R+D[x^y^z]); maximal values grow roughly quadratically (bounded by (a+1)(b+1) - 1). One match (L+R+D[x^y] diagonal 0, 2, 1, 1, 1, ... vs A137993) is a coincidence of an almost constant sequence.

Only 222 of 670 rows (a = 1..5, b < 1500) are additively periodic with period <= 375; 22 operations have all five rows periodic, 40 none. Row 2 of D[x^y] is the Jacobsthal block swap - an independent bitset recursion agrees with the mex table for b < 1500 and with the formula for every b < 2^15; it is an involution; neither the row nor |g(b) - b| is in the OEIS.
Row 2 of D[x^y] is not additively periodic (|f(2,b) - b| = J_k unbounded, Theorem 3)
No closed form is known to us for the odd values of G06; g(m)/m < 0.24985 for odd m <= 5000 (a bound m/4 is not proved).

new.novelty_basis: Elementary and implicit in the Imrich-Izbicki (1975) scheme of products defined by factor adjacencies; the full text of that paper was not consulted.
