new.statement:
For a local product S the canonical bijection ((g,h),k) -> (g,(h,k)) is an isomorphism (G*H)*K -> G*(H*K)
for all simple graphs G, H, K iff it is one for G = H = K = P3 iff phi_S(phi_S(r1,r2),r3) =
phi_S(r1,phi_S(r2,r3)) for all relations r1, r2, r3 in {E, A, N}. Likewise the swap is an isomorphism
G*H -> H*G for all G, H iff S is symmetric.
new.title: Associativity of a local graph product is a finite identity on relations, detected by P3 x P3 x P3 (Lean)

new.novelty_basis: W. Imrich, H. Izbicki, Associative products of graphs, Monatsh. Math. 80 (1975) 277-281, doi:10.1007/BF01472575 - exactly twenty associative products; R. J. Nowakowski, D. F. Rall, Discuss. Math. Graph Theory 16 (1996) 53-79, doi:10.7151/dmgt.1023 - ten depend on both factors, eight of those commutative. Our list agrees with both counts.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 kernel computation (assoc_codes, comm_assoc_codes by decide; standard axioms) on top of the Lean-verified reduction CLM-C14-01; independently in two Python implementations with graph-level brute force (EXP-C14-01, EXP-C14-06)
new.statement:
The associative local products are the codes 0, 1, 4, 5, 8, 13, 28, 29, 31, 73, 77, 85, 93, 109, 127, 141,
221, 223, 253, 255 (bit order EA, EN, AE, AA, AN, NE, NA, NN). The commutative ones among them are empty (0),
Cartesian (5), direct (8), strong (13), symmetric difference (85), co-normal (93), 127, 141, 221 and complete
(255). Exactly 8 have the two-sided unit K1: Cartesian, strong, lexicographic (29), its transpose (77),
symmetric difference, co-normal, 141, 221. They form 8 orbits under transposition and complement-conjugation.
new.title: Exactly 20 of the 256 local graph products are associative, 10 commutative, 8 with unit K1 (Lean decide)

new.novelty_basis: Bold hypothesis H-C14-1 of this cycle; whether Imrich-Izbicki or later work address isomorphism-level associativity could not be checked (abstracts only).
new.proof_check: computer-assisted - explicit witnesses for all 236 + 224 codes, each certified by edge count/degree sequence (hand-checkable), found in EXP-C14-02 and re-certified by the independent implementation of EXP-C14-06
new.statement:
A local product satisfies (G*H)*K isomorphic to G*(H*K) for all graphs iff it is strictly associative, and
G*H isomorphic to H*G for all graphs iff S is symmetric. For each of the 236 non-associative (224
non-commutative) products a witness exists with factors of at most 3 vertices whose two sides differ in edge
count or degree sequence.
new.title: For local graph products, associativity and commutativity up to isomorphism are no weaker than the strict notions

new.novelty_basis: The individual identities for the direct (A (x) B) and strong ((A+I) (x) (B+I)) products are classical and the co-normal one follows by complementation; we found no statement classifying the local products with such a linearisation, nor the symmetric-difference case in general (four web searches 2026-10-18, see CLM-C14-06). Small result; possibly folklore.
new.proof_check: written case analysis (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 4); polynomial system solved over C by sympy for all 256 codes (EXP-C14-03); Lean kernel computation for values in {-1,0,1} (character_codes); numerical matrix checks on random graphs
new.statement:
There is c = (cE, cA, cN) in C^3 with cA != cN and M_c(G*H) = M_c(G) (x) M_c(H) for all graphs, where
M_c(G) = cE I + cA A + cN (J - I - A), exactly for: direct (c = (0,1,0), M = A), code 127 (0,0,1),
strong (1,1,0), co-normal (1,0,1), symmetric difference (1,-1,1), M = S(G) + I with S the Seidel matrix,
and code 141 (1,1,-1), M = I - S(G); the character is unique in each case, and every such product is
associative and commutative.
new.title: Exactly six local products are Kronecker products in disguise (multiplicative characters)

new.novelty_basis: The Kronecker-sum formula for the Cartesian product is classical; the classification over all 256 local products was not found (same searches as CLM-C14-04). Small result.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 5); sympy over C for all 256 codes (EXP-C14-03)
new.statement:
M_c(G*H) = M_c(G) (x) I + I (x) M_c(H) for all graphs (cA != cN) holds exactly for the Cartesian product
(c = (0,t,0)) and code 221 (c = (0,0,t)), t != 0. Hence each of the ten commutative associative local
products except the empty and the complete product has exactly one kind of character (multiplicative or
additive).
new.title: Additive characters: only the Cartesian product and its complement-dual; every non-trivial commutative associative product has a character

new.novelty_basis: Searches (2026-10-18): 'symmetric difference' + Seidel spectrum; Kronecker product of Seidel matrices / two-graphs; tensor product of two-graphs. Only the special case with an edgeless factor, S(D_m(G)) + I = J_m (x) (S(G) + I), was found (a paper on Seidel equienergetic graphs, seen through a secondary summary). The symmetric-difference product itself is Harary-Wilcox (1967). One-line observation; plausibly known to two-graph specialists.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 6); entry-level identity in Lean (xor_character); exact integer check for all pairs of graphs with <= 3 vertices (EXP-C14-06); spectra on 30 random pairs (EXP-C14-03)
new.statement:
For all graphs G, H: S(G xor H) + I = (S(G) + I) (x) (S(H) + I), where xor is the symmetric-difference product
and S the Seidel matrix. Hence the Seidel eigenvalues of G xor H are (theta+1)(eta+1) - 1, and xor is
compatible with Seidel switching, giving a commutative associative product on two-graphs with unit [K1].
new.title: The symmetric-difference product is the Kronecker product of Seidel matrices; it acts on two-graphs

new.novelty_basis: No statement found in the searches listed for CLM-C14-06. Small result.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 7; (c) via twin reducts of +-1 matrices); (a) checked edge by edge for a,b,c,d <= 4, (b) on 200 random cases (EXP-C14-06); (c) on 12,713 pairs with <= 6 vertices (EXP-C14-05)
new.statement:
(a) K_{a,b} xor K_{c,d} = K_{ac+bd, ad+bc}; so (|V|, |a-b|) is multiplicative on complete bipartite graphs.
(b) K_{a,a} xor X is isomorphic to K_{a,a} xor X^Z for every switching X^Z of X (a >= 1).
(c) K2 xor X is isomorphic to K2 xor Y iff X and Y are switching-equivalent.
new.title: Complete bipartite graphs multiply as (order, imbalance); K2 absorbs Seidel switching

new.counterexample: Symmetric difference: K2 xor K2 xor K2 is isomorphic to K2 xor K_{1,3}; K2 and K_{1,3} are connected and prime, so this connected graph of order 8 has the two factorisations {K2,K2,K2} and {K2,K_{1,3}} (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 8; explicit isomorphism in EXP-C14-06). In all graphs already C4 = K2 xor K2 = K2 xor 2K1. The other five products show no collision up to order 15 in the stated classes, consistent with Sabidussi-Vizing and Doerfler-Imrich/McKenzie.
new.statement:
Each of the six commutative associative local products with unit K1 (Cartesian, strong, symmetric
difference, and their complement-duals 221, co-normal, 141) has unique prime factorisation on connected
graphs, or, for the complement-duals, on co-connected graphs.
new.title: H-C14-3: the six commutative unital associative products factor uniquely on connected (or co-connected) graphs (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Connected Cartesian primes = OEIS A129582 (Ji Li, Prime graphs and exponential composition of species, J. Combin. Theory A 115 (2008) 1374-1401, arXiv:0705.0038). The semiring view of disconnected graphs and the parallel cancellation theory for Cartesian and strong products are in Hammack-Imrich-Klavzar's Handbook and Klavzar et al., Cancellation properties of products of graphs; the isomorphism statement is a reformulation.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C14.md Theorem 9) relying on the published unique factorisation theorems for connected graphs (Sabidussi-Vizing; Doerfler-Imrich/McKenzie); census confirms equal counts for n <= 15 and reproduces A129582 to n = 15
new.statement:
There is an order-preserving monoid isomorphism between (finite graphs, Cartesian product) and (finite graphs,
strong product), and by complementation between the co-normal product and code 221; for every n the four
products have the same number of prime graphs of order n, and the connected Cartesian and strong primes are
equinumerous (OEIS A129582).
new.title: The Cartesian and strong product monoids of all finite graphs are isomorphic graded monoids; equal prime counts (A129582)

new.novelty_basis: OEIS searches (cached, 2026-10-18) found none of the three sequences; derived sequences of a natural kind, novelty unconfirmed.
new.proof_check: computer-assisted exact census (all prime factorisations of each order <= 15 with factors from the complete list of graphs with <= 7 vertices, isomorphism decided by VF2 within invariant buckets; graph totals from OEIS A000088); pipeline validated by reproducing A129582 to n = 15
new.statement:
Prime graphs of order n = 2..11 over all finite graphs: Cartesian = strong = co-normal = code 221:
2, 4, 8, 34, 148, 1044, 12326, 274658, 12005100, 1018997864; symmetric difference = code 141:
2, 4, 9, 34, 150, 1044, 12333, 274658, 12005127, 1018997864; lexicographic = its transpose:
2, 4, 7, 34, 142, 1044, 12310, 274652, 12005036, 1018997864 (values to n = 15 in results/EXP-C14-04.json).
new.title: Numbers of prime graphs (all graphs) for the unital associative products, orders <= 15

new.novelty_basis: Non-uniqueness of lexicographic prime factorisation (with an invariant number of factors) is due to Imrich; cited via arXiv:2407.02615 and the Handbook of Product Graphs. The specific minimal example was not looked up.
new.proof_check: by hand (both sides are two disjoint 4-cycles plus two isolated vertices); minimality by the exact census EXP-C14-04
new.statement:
2K1[C4 + K1] and (2K2 + K1)[2K1] are both isomorphic to 2C4 + 2K1; C4 + K1 and 2K2 + K1 are prime (order 5),
so 2C4 + 2K1 has two lexicographic factorisations with different multisets of prime factors. No such
collision occurs below order 10.
new.title: The lexicographic product has non-unique factorisation already at order 10 (different multisets of primes)

new.limitations: Exhaustive only for orders <= 15 inside the submonoid of connected graphs (factors with <= 7 vertices); the mechanism that breaks uniqueness for connected graphs under xor (absorption of switching by K2, Theorem 7) is unavailable because 2K1 is disconnected, which explains but does not prove the observation.
new.statement:
Every connected graph has exactly one factorisation into connected primes with respect to the product
(g,h) ~ (g',h') iff (EA, AE, AA or NN); equivalently every graph with connected complement factors uniquely
under the symmetric-difference product into primes with connected complement.
new.title: Code 141 (EA AE AA NN) has unique factorisation on connected graphs (equivalently, symmetric difference on co-connected graphs)

new.limitations: No collision among all factorisations of orders <= 16 (orders 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16); class counts validated against A002854 for n <= 8. Prime two-graph counts (exact for n <= 16): 1, 2, 2, 7, 14, 54, 240, 2035, 33113, ... Cancellation by [K2] is proved (CLM-C14-07c).
new.novelty_basis: No source found for a product of two-graphs induced by the symmetric difference (searches listed under CLM-C14-06); OEIS has no match for the prime counts.
new.statement:
Every switching class of finite graphs has a unique factorisation into prime switching classes with respect
to the product induced by the symmetric difference (equivalently, symmetric +-1 matrices with unit diagonal
up to signed permutation similarity, under the Kronecker product).
new.title: H-C14-4: two-graphs form a free commutative monoid under the symmetric-difference (Kronecker) product

new: Exhaustive classification of the 256 local products: exactly 20 are associative (10 of them commutative; 32 symmetric products in total); exactly 8 have the two-sided unit K1 (Cartesian, strong, lexicographic and its transpose, symmetric difference, co-normal, codes 141 and 221); associative and distributive over disjoint union on both sides: codes 0, 1, 4, Cartesian, direct, strong. The relation-level verdict agrees with brute-force graph computations (P3^3 and 40 random triples per code) for every code; the 20 associative products form 8 orbits under transposition and complement-conjugation.

Every one of the 236 non-associative products has a witness (G*H)*K not isomorphic to G*(H*K) with factors of at most 3 vertices (product orders 2: 144 codes, 4: 84, 8: 8), and every one of the 224 non-commutative products a witness G*H not isomorphic to H*G; all 460 witnesses are certified by edge count or degree sequence. Associativity and commutativity up to isomorphism are therefore no weaker than the strict notions (bold H-C14-1 survives).

The character equations solved over C (sympy) for all 256 codes give exactly six multiplicative characters - direct (0,1,0), strong (1,1,0), symmetric difference (1,-1,1), co-normal (1,0,1), code 127 (0,0,1), code 141 (1,1,-1) - and exactly two additive ones - Cartesian (0,t,0) and code 221 (0,0,t); identical to the hand case analysis; 0 numerical failures of the matrix identities on 30 random pairs per product; the Seidel spectrum of symmetric-difference products is multiplicative (shifted by 1) on 30/30 pairs. Only the empty and complete products among the 10 commutative associative ones have no character.

Exact factorisation census for the 8 unital associative products, orders <= 15 (factors: all graphs with <= 7 vertices). All graphs: Cartesian, strong, co-normal and 221 have no collision; lexicographic and its transpose collide at orders 10 and 14 as multisets (e.g. 2K1 o (C4+K1) = (2K2+K1) o 2K1); symmetric difference and 141 collide at orders 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15 (1, 2, 3, 7, 16, 54, 1 classes). Inside connected graphs the symmetric difference collides at orders 8, 10, 12, 14 (2, 6, 15, 53 classes: K2 xor K2 xor K2 = K2 xor K_{1,3}) - H-C14-3 refuted - while code 141 (equivalently XOR on co-connected graphs) has none. Connected Cartesian and strong prime counts both equal OEIS A129582 for n = 2..15; prime counts over all graphs computed for every product (no OEIS match). The classical 63-vertex Cartesian/strong counterexample for disconnected graphs was verified.
Symmetric difference: K2 xor K2 xor K2 is isomorphic to K2 xor K_{1,3} (connected, order 8); C4 = K2 xor K2 = K2 xor 2K1 (order 4)

Switching classes of order <= 8 reproduce OEIS A002854 (1, 1, 2, 3, 7, 16, 54, 243). Under the symmetric difference no two-graph of order <= 16 has two factorisations into prime two-graphs (composite classes 1, 2, 3, 3, 7, 20, 54, 14, 246 at orders 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, each with exactly one factorisation); prime two-graph counts 1, 2, 2, 7, 14, 54, 240, 2035, 33113, ... (n = 2, 3, ...), not in the OEIS. K2 xor X = K2 xor Y holds exactly for switching-equivalent X, Y on all 12,713 pairs of graphs with <= 6 vertices.

Skeptic's re-implementation sharing no code with systems/graph_products.py reproduces the 20/10 classification, re-certifies all 460 non-isomorphism witnesses, finds an explicit isomorphism K2 xor K2 xor K2 -> K2 xor K_{1,3} and K2 xor K2 -> K2 xor 2K1, checks K_{a,b} xor K_{c,d} = K_{ac+bd, ad+bc} edge by edge for a, b, c, d <= 4, the identity S(G xor H) + I = (S(G)+I) (x) (S(H)+I) exactly in integers for all pairs of graphs with <= 3 vertices, and K2 xor X = K2 xor X^Z on 200 random cases. No discrepancy.

Spectra of symmetric-difference (Seidel), strong (A+I), co-normal (J-A) and Cartesian (A) products obtained from the factors agree with direct diagonalisation to relative error 1.2e-14 in all 16 cases (n = m <= 40); at nm = 1600 the factor route took about 0.2-0.4 ms against 14-19 s for numpy.linalg.eigvalsh on the shared, heavily loaded machine (absolute times inflated by load; the gain is the standard Kronecker O((nm)^3) -> O(n^3 + m^3 + nm log nm)).

new.falsification: A non-affine anchored model of any selected law.

new.question: For laws whose affine spectrum is infinite but not all N (golden, x^2+x+1, -1 square, 2 square, odd, plastic, tribonacci, ...), does every anchored model of size N <= 8 come from an affine table x*y = x + a*y + 1? If so, the true spectrum agrees with the arithmetic set for N <= 8.
new.title: Affine rigidity of laws with infinite non-trivial affine spectra

assumptions: light cones to t = 18 (tables of 2^19 entries)
cyclic rows of length L = 1..16
surjectivity and injectivity on bi-infinite rows by the pair-graph (Garden of Eden) criterion

Le Floch's notes 'Spectrum of equational laws' (Lean Zulip upload spectrum.pdf) discuss every law with possibly non-full spectrum; our census agrees with every spectrum fragment stated there for the laws concerned.
new.statement:
Of the 115 identities t = x (x occurring in t, neither leftmost nor rightmost), 52 have models of every order
1..6, 2 have none of orders 2..6, and 61 have restricted spectra; the 63 non-full ones fall into 15 patterns
on n = 1..8 listed in research/cycles/C05_magma_spectra/README.md (e.g. 10111011 for 16 identities including
the Dupont law, 10110010 = Mendelsohn pattern for law 66 and three equivalents, 1010001? for law 907).
new.title: Spectrum census of the 115 nontrivial two-variable identities t = x with 2-4 operations (n <= 6, restricted ones to n <= 8)

new.statement: If x occurs in t but is neither its leftmost nor its rightmost leaf, every finite model of t = x is a quasigroup.
new.title: H-C05-Q: nontrivial identities t = x force their finite models to be quasigroups (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Proposition 3 of the ETP write-up 'Spectra of order-3 equations' (Lean Zulip upload; attributed in Le Floch's notes to Ben Gunby-Mann) gives the same orbit argument and the full spectrum. Our addition is a Lean formalisation of the necessity half via a fixed-point-free involution on Sym2.

new.statement:
If a finite magma satisfies x = (y*x)*(x*y) for all x, y, its order n satisfies n = 0 or 1 (mod 4).
(With the constructions of the ETP write-up "Spectra of order-3 equations" the spectrum is exactly
{n : n = 0, 1 mod 4}.)
new.title: Law 167, x = (y*x)*(x*y): every finite model has order 0 or 1 mod 4

new.novelty_basis: Standard finite-set argument (a surjective self-map of a finite set is bijective), used throughout the ETP notes.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the x = y*s(x,y) case (left_mul_bijective_of_law); the general path version by written proof
new.statement:
If a finite magma satisfies x = y * s(x, y) for some binary term operation s, every left translation a -> y*a
is a bijection (every row of the Cayley table is a permutation). More generally, in a finite model of t = x
with x occurring once in t, every translation on the path from the root of t to x is a bijection.
new.title: Identities x = y*s(x, y) make every left translation of a finite model bijective

new.counterexample: x = (y*x)*(x*(y*y)) has models of every order 1..6 (EXP-C05-01); of order 2 it is satisfied by NAND (Lean: nand2_law), yet no affine operation over Z_2 satisfies it (Lean: no_affine_model_mod2); its affine models exist only for n in {1, 5}. Three further identities behave alike (EXP-C05-05).
new.statement: A nontrivial identity t = x has models of all orders 1..6 iff it has an affine model x*y = a x + b y + c over Z_n for every n <= 6.
new.title: H-C05-A: full spectrum iff affine models over every Z_n (refuted)

No magma of the stated order satisfies: 501 x = y(y(x(xy))) - orders 2, 3, 6, 7; 677 x = y(x((yx)y)) - orders

new.statement: The finite models of x = y(x((yx)y)) (ETP 677) and of x = y(((yx)x)y) (ETP 1313) have exactly the orders 1 and the odd integers n >= 5.
new.title: Laws 677 and 1313 have spectrum {1} together with all odd n >= 5

new: All 115 nontrivial two-variable identities t = x with 2-4 operations were decided for n = 1..6 except law 167 at n = 6 (UNKNOWN within budget; excluded by the Lean theorem). 61 have restricted spectra, 52 are full on 1..6, 2 admit only n = 1 there; mirror pairs always agree; 18 identities have non-quasigroup models of order <= 3.

The 63 non-full identities fall into 15 spectrum patterns on n = 1..8, reproducing every spectrum fragment stated in the ETP notes for the laws concerned; 52/63 have only quasigroup models for n <= 5; the Dupont family (16 identities incl. laws 63, 115) has a single, medial model class at each of n = 3, 4, 5. The 'identical model set' grouping in this run compared non-canonical representatives and is not used (defect recorded).

15 laws with unknown spectrum in the ETP notes decided for n <= 10 except a few sizes (UNKNOWN at budget 1e6); zero disagreements with the notes. The field decided_beyond_notes lists sizes not literally enumerated in the notes; the README table separates the facts genuinely absent from the notes.

Published theorem - for every N there is a unique operation on {1..N} with p*1 = p+1 mod N and p*(q+1) = (p*q)*(p+1) for q < N (the recursion without its wrap-around instance), and it is left-distributive iff N is a power of 2 (R. Laver 1992/1995; elementary proof in A. Drapal's survey; see P. Dehornoy, Braids and Self-Distributivity (2000), Ch. X; P. Dehornoy, 'Some aspects of the SD-world', arXiv:1711.09792; P. Biane, arXiv:1810.00548). Lean checks A_3 and the non-existence for N = 3 (laver3_left_distributive, no_anchored_ld_three); the general theorem is not re-proved by the lab.
old: Published theorem - for every N there is a unique operation on {1..N} with p*1 = p+1 mod N and p*(q*1) = (p*q)*(p*1), and it is left-distributive iff N is a power of 2 (R. Laver 1992/1995; elementary proof in A. Drapal's survey; see P. Dehornoy, Braids and Self-Distributivity (2000), Ch. X; P. Dehornoy, 'Some aspects of the SD-world', arXiv:1711.09792; P. Biane, arXiv:1810.00548). Lean checks A_3 and the non-existence for N = 3 (laver3_left_distributive, no_anchored_ld_three); the general theorem is not re-proved by the lab.
reason: Wording of the cited theorem corrected - the recursion is imposed for q < N only; EXP-C17-02 shows that with the wrap-around instance there are no anchored solutions at N = 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10

new.novelty_basis: F. W. Light's associativity test, presented in A. H. Clifford, G. B. Preston, The Algebraic Theory of Semigroups, Vol. 1 (AMS, 1961), section 1.2.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C17.md Theorem 1, four-line closure argument); 0 wrong verdicts in EXP-C17-01; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: If S generates the finite magma M, then M is associative iff (x*s)*y = x*(s*y) for all x, y in M and s in S; the test costs 2n + 2n^2 probes per generator.
new.title: Light's test: generators suffice for associativity

new.novelty_basis: Immediate from Light's test and the lab's C06 Theorem 1; small.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C17.md Corollary 2) from C06 Theorem 1 (Lean anchored_assoc_unique); 0 wrong verdicts on 30 anchored instances (EXP-C17-01)
new.statement: If x*0 = x + 1 (mod n), then * is associative iff x*(y + 1) = (x*y) + 1 for all x, y (2n^2 probes); equivalently Light's test with the single generator 0.
new.title: Associativity of an anchored magma is decided by one O(n^2) identity

new.novelty_basis: S. Rajagopalan, L. J. Schulman, Verification of identities, SIAM J. Comput. 29 (2000) 1155-1168.
new.proof_check: one-sidedness proved (proofs/paper/C17.md Theorem 3, bilinear extension); the 1/8 detection bound is the cited theorem of Rajagopalan-Schulman, not re-proved; empirically 0 errors in 90 instances with 40 rounds
new.statement: The GF(2) subset-sum test (compare (u*v)*w and u*(v*w) in the magma algebra for random subsets u, v, w) never rejects an associative table, and rejects a non-associative one with probability at least 1/8 per round; each round costs O(n^2) probes.
new.title: The Rajagopalan-Schulman randomised associativity test is one-sided

new.limitations: Families chosen to include worst cases for each method; no comparison with optimised C implementations.
new.novelty_basis: The algorithms are classical (Light; Rajagopalan-Schulman); the benchmark is ours. Timings were measured on a shared, loaded machine and are indicative only; probe counts are exact.
new.statement: On cyclic groups, anchored tables, random magmas and their one-entry corruptions (n = 32..512), Light's test with a greedy generating set uses 23-614 times fewer table probes than the exhaustive n^3 check (generating-set cost included) and the anchored test 2n^2 probes; on left-zero bands the gain is only 1.7x. The randomised test (40 rounds) made no error; random-triple sampling with n^2/16 samples missed 27 of 30 near-associative inputs.
new.title: Benchmark - generator and anchor tests versus the exhaustive check

new.limitations: Complete SAT enumeration for N <= 10 only.
new.novelty_basis: Probably a consequence of known Laver-table theory (row N is the identity and p*N = N exactly for powers of 2); not checked against the literature.
new.statement: For 2 <= N <= 10, an anchored magma satisfies x*(y+1) = (x*y)*(x+1) for all x, y mod N exactly when N is 2, 4 or 8 and the magma is the Laver table; so for these N, left-distributivity of an anchored table is decided by an O(N^2) check.
new.title: The anchor instance of left-distributivity singles out the Laver tables (N <= 10)

new.counterexample: Left-zero band x*y = x (n generators needed): ratio 1.7 at n = 512; also one-entry corruptions of cyclic groups (ratio 47.9 < 51.2 at n = 512, because the exhaustive check stops at the first violation).
new.statement: Light's test with a greedy generating set uses at most a fraction 10/n of the exhaustive check's probes on every input family.
new.title: H-C17-1: Light's test beats the exhaustive check by a factor >= n/10 on every family (refuted)

new.counterexample: 18 laws, e.g. x(yz) = y(y(xz)) (two violating models among 11 at N = 4), x(yz) = x((xy)z), (xy)z = (zy)x, (xy)z = (x(zz))y (EXP-C17-02). It does hold for associativity and (N <= 10) for left-distributivity.
new.statement: For every law of the C06 family, every anchored magma satisfying the instance z = 0 of the law satisfies the law (N <= 5).
new.title: H-C17-2: for anchored magmas the z = 0 instance of a law decides the law (refuted)

new: All Light, anchored and Rajagopalan-Schulman (40 rounds) verdicts are correct on 90 instances (n = 32..512). In table probes the exhaustive check costs 23-614 times more than Light's test with a greedy generating set (generating-set cost included), except on left-zero bands (x*y = x, every element is a generator), where the ratio is only 1.7. Random-triple sampling with n^2/16 samples misses 27 of the 30 inputs that differ from an associative table in one entry (about 4n bad triples out of n^3). At n = 512 (shared machine, indicative) - exhaustive 1.4-1.7 s for associative inputs, Light 2-3 ms + 3 ms for the generating set, anchored test 3 ms, RS(40) 0.2 s.
left-zero band x*y = x: Light's test needs n generators and is only 1.7x cheaper than the exhaustive check (H-C17-1 refuted)

For the 382 laws of C06, the instance z = 0 of the law (with the anchor) implies the full law in every anchored model for N = 2..5 for 333 laws, is insufficient for 18, and could not be decided by enumeration for 31 (more than 3000 models). Associativity - the instance alone forces x*y = x + y + 1. Left-distributivity - the wrap-around instance x*(y+1) = (x*y)*(x+1) has solutions only for N = 2, 4, 8 (N <= 10), each the Laver table.
x(yz) = y(y(xz)): the anchor instance has 11 anchored models at N = 4, two of which violate the law (190 models, 114 violating, at N = 5)

large gains when a small generating set exists (up to 614x fewer probes; on associative inputs at n = 512 Light incl. generating set is 235-340x faster and the anchored test 565x faster than the exhaustive check, indicative timings); essentially none on left-zero bands (1.7x); randomised tests trade certainty for O(n^2) cost

new.falsification: H-C15-1: a magma with growing but sub-geometric width. H-C15-2: a bounded-width magma outside the three classes or a semigroup/affine magma with unbounded width. H-C15-3: a surjective non-permutive table or a non-surjective permutive one.
new.hypothesis: H-C15-1 (bold, inventor): no intermediate growth - the streaming width lambda(t) (the smaller of the forward and backward ordered-BDD widths of F_t) is either eventually constant (lambda(7) = lambda(8) = lambda(9)) or grows at least geometrically (lambda(t+2) >= 2 lambda(t), t = 5, 6, 7). H-C15-2 (bold, inventor): bounded streaming width holds exactly for semigroups, affine magmas x*y = ax + by + c over Z_3, and magmas whose light cone depends on at most two cells. H-C15-3 (explorer): the automaton is surjective on bi-infinite rows iff the table has all rows or all columns permutations (permutive).
new.methodology: Canonical representatives by minimum code over the 12 (anti-)relabellings; for each: algebraic properties, essential variables and widths of F_t (t <= 9), nilpotency, pair-graph surjectivity and injectivity, functional-graph statistics of the global map on cyclic rows.
new.question: For all 1734 magmas of order 3 up to isomorphism and anti-isomorphism: how complex are the t-step local maps of c'_i = c_i * c_{i+1}, which automata are surjective, and how do they behave on cyclic rows?
new.title: Order-3 magma automata: light cones, streaming widths, surjectivity and cyclic dynamics

spectra up to 200 from the root condition; OEIS lookups for the distinct polynomials

N = 1..12, complete SAT (conflict budget 2,000,000; UNKNOWN recorded)

assumptions: all 16 tables of order 2 and all 19683 of order 3; for order 4 only the (4!)^4 = 331776 tables whose rows are permutations (the only candidates for a full cycle by H-C16-2)
isomorphism classes by brute-force canonical codes (n <= 3; full-period tables for n = 4)
the mirror recurrence x_{k+1} = x_{k-1} * x_k is the forward recurrence of the transposed table; checked on the order-3 census
new.falsification: H-C16-1: a table with a period n^2, or a non-quasigroup attaining the maximum. H-C16-2: a permutation pair map with a non-bijective left translation or vice versa, or a count different from (n!)^n. H-C16-3: a full-period count different from (n!)^n / n^2.
new.hypothesis: H-C16-1 (bold, Inventor): as for Pisano periods, where (0, 0) is fixed, the maximal period on an n-element magma is at most n^2 - 1, and the maximum is attained only by quasigroups. H-C16-2 (Formal Verifier): the pair map is a permutation iff every left translation a -> b*a is a bijection, so exactly (n!)^n tables give permutations. H-C16-3 (Formal Verifier, after the n = 2 data): the tables with a single cycle through all n^2 states correspond to de Bruijn cycles of order 2, (n!)^n / n^2 of them (1, 24, 20736 for n = 2, 3, 4).
new.methodology: Batch functional-graph analysis (orbit doubling, periods, transients) of the pair maps; count permutation pair maps and full-period tables; test the quasigroup property of the full-period tables; distributions of the maximal period; OEIS check of the counts.
new.question: How long can the sequence x_{k+1} = x_k * x_{k-1} cycle in an n-element magma, when is the pair map a permutation, and which magmas attain the longest periods?
new.title: Cycle structure of the Fibonacci pair map (a, b) -> (b, b*a) for all small magmas

the 8 rules of the two symmetry classes (reversal, letter exchange) are checked separately
new.falsification: A word whose strategies give different lengths (would contradict random descent), a word whose derivation does not end within 10^6 steps, or any mismatch with the formulas.

new.title: C03 Conjecture 4.6 versus the Zantema-Geser characterisation - not settled (full text inaccessible)

new: All 8 rules of the two classes aab -> ababa and aab -> babaa terminate on every word of length <= 12 (rightmost and leftmost strategies agree on every word, and agree with the exact maximal derivation length on all words of length <= 8, as random descent predicts). D(n) for aab -> ababa is 0, 0, 1, 3, 7, ..., 1023 = 2^(n-2) - 1; for aab -> babaa 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 21, 30, 45, 62 = max_b b(2^floor((n-b)/2) - 1); the per-word formula for aab -> babaa matches every word of length <= 12.

new.novelty_basis: Pascal's triangle for additive CA is classical (Martin, Odlyzko, Wolfram, Comm. Math. Phys. 93 (1984)); automata of the form c'_i = c_i * c_{i+1} over groupoids, groups and quasigroups were studied by J. Pedersen (Complex Systems 6 (1992) 237-250) and C. Moore (Moore-Drisko 1995/96; Moore-Pnin, arXiv:patt-sol/9701008), where the word structure of semigroup and group rules is used. The width bound is immediate.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the commutative formula (ca_comm_binomial, ca_step_shift; standard axioms only); written proof for the word form and the width bound (proofs/paper/C15.md Theorem 1); every order-3 semigroup has width <= 3 (EXP-C15-02); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
For an associative magma the t-step local map is the ordered product F_t(x_0..x_t) = prod_{j < 2^t} x_{s(j)},
s(j) the binary digit sum of j; for a commutative semigroup F_t = prod_k x_k^C(t,k), and the forward and
backward streaming widths of F_t are at most |S|.
new.title: Light cones of semigroups - the popcount word, Pascal exponents, bounded streaming width

new.novelty_basis: Linear and affine cellular automata (O. Martin, A. M. Odlyzko, S. Wolfram, Algebraic properties of cellular automata, Comm. Math. Phys. 93 (1984) 219-258; M. Ito, N. Osato, M. Nasu 1983); the operator-power form is standard.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C15.md Theorem 2); implementation agrees with direct simulation in all 55 affine cases (EXP-C15-03); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
For x*y = phi(x) + psi(y) + c on an abelian group A with commuting endomorphisms phi, psi:
F_t = sum_k C(t,k) phi^(t-k) psi^k (x_k) + sum_(s<t) (phi + psi)^s (c); on cyclic rows the row at time t is
P^t r + (sum_(s<t) q^s) c with P = phi + psi S in End(A)[S]/(S^L - 1), computable by binary exponentiation
(for A = Z_n with FFT products, O(L log L log t)); streaming width <= |A|.
new.title: Affine magmas - binomial light cone and an O(L log L log t) fast-forward

new.novelty_basis: A direct combination of Theorem 1(b) with the index/period structure of cyclic semigroups; likely folklore.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C15.md Theorem 3); implementation agrees with direct simulation for three commutative semigroups (EXP-C15-03); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: For a finite commutative semigroup and t >= 2L + iota + 1 (iota the largest index of an element), cell i of a cyclic row at time t is prod_j r_(i+j)^(N_j), where N_j are the coefficients of (1 + S)^t mod S^L - 1, and only N_j modulo the lcm of the element periods is needed.
new.title: Commutative semigroups - fast-forward by exponent arithmetic

new.novelty_basis: Searches (2026-10-18) on CA prediction complexity, branching-program/light-cone complexity and computational irreducibility (Wolfram; Israeli-Goldenfeld, arXiv:nlin/0309047; Moore's prediction papers) found no notion of streaming width of t-step rules and no analysis of this rule; the burn-time mechanism itself is elementary. Small.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C15.md Theorem 4); fast-forward agrees with direct simulation on 27,000 (row, t) pairs during development and in all EXP-C15-03 cases; widths and the lower-bound residual family checked to t = 12 (EXP-C15-05); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
For the fuse magma [[0,0,0],[0,0,1],[1,2,2]] (0 burnt, 1 burning, 2 intact): burn times satisfy tau_i = 0 (x_i = 0),
tau_(i+1) + 2 (x_i = 2), tau_(i+1) (x_i = 1, x_(i+1) = 2), 1 (x_i = 1, x_(i+1) != 2); the row at any time t is
obtained from them in O(L) operations; and floor((m+1)/2) <= lambda(t) <= 3t + 3 with m = floor(t/2), so the
streaming width grows linearly (computed lambda(t) = t + 2 for t <= 12).
new.title: The fuse magma: linear streaming width, yet an O(L) fast-forward for every t

new.novelty_basis: J. Kari, V. Salo, I. Torma, Surjective two-neighbor cellular automata on prime alphabets (2013) - surjective two-neighbour CA over prime alphabets are permutive in some coordinate (https://research.utu.fi/converis/portal/detail/Publication/3119276; notes https://villesalo.com/notes/STNCAoPANotes.html); G. A. Hedlund, Math. Systems Theory 3 (1969). Our exhaustive check is an independent confirmation for n = 2, 3; the order-4 band illustrates why primality is needed.
new.proof_check: computer-assisted - exact pair-graph (Garden-of-Eden) decision for all 16 tables of order 2 and all 1734 classes of order 3 (invariant under isomorphism and mirror image), Hedlund's theorem for permutive => surjective; the order-4 example by a two-line argument (identity x shift) and the same decision procedure (EXP-C15-05)
new.statement: For |M| <= 3 the automaton c'_i = c_i * c_{i+1} is surjective on bi-infinite rows iff all rows or all columns of the table are permutations (1, 6, 420 surjective tables of orders 1, 2, 3 = 2(n!)^n - Lat(n)); for |M| = 4 the rectangular band (b,c)*(b',c') = (b,c') is surjective and injective but not permutive.
new.title: Surjective iff permutive for magmas of order at most 3; false at order 4

new.novelty_basis: Elementary-rule numbering (S. Wolfram, Rev. Mod. Phys. 55 (1983)); rules independent of one neighbour are a standard subfamily.
new.proof_check: written one-line proof (proofs/paper/C15.md Theorem 6) and exhaustive computation (EXP-C15-01)
new.statement: The 16 automata of two-element magmas are exactly the elementary cellular automata whose rule ignores the left neighbour, the Wolfram numbers 0, 17, 34, ..., 255.
new.title: The two-element magma automata are the elementary rules 17m

new.limitations: Growth classes are judged on t <= 9 only and may change for larger t; 'linear' and 'geometric' are empirical labels except for the fuse magma (Theorem 4).
new.novelty_basis: Same searches as CLM-C15-04; the magma-automaton framework itself is Pedersen's (1992) and Moore's, but no census of this kind was found. Low confidence.
new.statement: Of the 1734 order-3 magma automata (up to isomorphism and mirror image), on t <= 9 the streaming width is bounded for 808 classes, grows linearly for 104, geometrically for 300 (largest lambda(9) = 649) and irregularly for 522; 43 are surjective, 7 injective and 34 nilpotent by t = 9.
new.title: Census of order-3 magma automata by streaming width

new.counterexample: The fuse magma [[0,0,0],[0,0,1],[1,2,2]] has floor((floor(t/2)+1)/2) <= lambda(t) <= 3t + 3 (Theorem 4; lambda(t) = t + 2 for t <= 12); 104 order-3 classes show linear growth on t <= 9 (EXP-C15-02).
new.statement: For every magma automaton of order <= 3 the streaming width lambda(t) is either bounded or grows geometrically; there is no intermediate growth.
new.title: H-C15-1: streaming width is either bounded or geometric (refuted)

new.counterexample: The 'if' direction holds for all 18 semigroup and 8 affine classes, but 685 bounded-width classes lie outside the three classes, e.g. the reversible automaton [[0,0,2],[2,2,0],[1,1,1]] whose light cone uses all t + 1 cells and whose width stays 3 (EXP-C15-02).
new.statement: An order-3 magma automaton has bounded streaming width iff the magma is a semigroup, is affine over Z_3, or its light cone depends on at most two cells.
new.title: H-C15-2: bounded width exactly for semigroups, affine magmas and bounded light cones (refuted)

new.counterexample: The fuse magma has unbounded (linear) streaming width but its row at any time t is computable in O(L) operations (Theorem 4). The converse direction is open (CLM-C15-18).
new.statement: A magma automaton admits a fast-forward (rows at time t computable in time polynomial in L and log t) if and only if its streaming width is bounded.
new.title: H-C15-4: an automaton can be fast-forwarded iff its light-cone complexity is bounded (refuted)

new.counterexample: The first part holds (1590/1734 classes at L = 32), the second fails - the bounded-width affine quasigroups x + y, 2x + y, 2x + 2y, 2x + 2y + 1 (mod 3, up to relabelling) do not repeat within 5000 steps at L = 32 and 64 (EXP-C15-04).
new.statement: For at least half of the order-3 classes a random cyclic row of length 32 repeats within 5000 steps, and only classes with geometric streaming width have rows that do not.
new.title: H-C15-5: cycle detection fast-forwards most automata, and long cycles mean geometric width (refuted in part)

new.counterexample: Exactness holds (99/99), but the commutative-semigroup method reaches only x62 (mult mod 3) and x77 (min) at L = 1024, t = 10^5, while the affine and fuse methods are already 1.4-6.4x faster at t = 100 for every L in {256, 1024, 4096} (EXP-C15-03; indicative timings).
new.statement: Each of the affine, commutative-semigroup and fuse fast-forwards is exact, beats direct numpy simulation by more than 100x at L = 1024, t = 10^5, and loses for t below a few hundred steps.
new.title: H-C15-6: every exact fast-forward beats simulation by more than 100x at L = 1024, t = 10^5 and loses for small t (refuted)

new.improvement_detail: against direct numpy simulation (O(L t)); asymptotically O(L log L log t) vs O(L t); indicative timings on a shared machine
new.novelty_basis: Standard for linear CA (Martin-Odlyzko-Wolfram 1984); the benchmark is ours.
new.statement: Computing the row at time t of an affine magma automaton by binary exponentiation of P = a + bS modulo S^L - 1 (FFT products) is exact and, at L = 1024, about 3-4x faster than direct numpy simulation at t = 100, 22-29x at 10^3, 138-215x at 10^4 and 1800-2500x at 10^5; t = 10^9 takes 1.5-8 ms for L <= 4096.
new.title: Affine fast-forward by operator powers

new.improvement_detail: wins only for t much larger than L; the O(L^2) product step dominates for moderate t
new.statement: The exponent-arithmetic fast-forward (Theorem 3) is exact; at L = 1024 it is 62-100x faster than direct simulation at t = 10^5 but 0.5-0.9x (slower) around t = 10^3 for L >= 1024, and equal for t < 2L (where it falls back to simulation).
new.title: Commutative-semigroup fast-forward by exponent arithmetic

new.improvement_detail: O(L) per query independent of t vs O(L t) simulation; indicative timings
new.novelty_basis: As CLM-C15-04.
new.statement: The burn-time fast-forward of the fuse magma (Theorem 4) is exact and takes O(L) time for every t - 1.4-5.3x faster than direct simulation at t = 100 (L = 256-4096) and about 4000x at t = 10^5 (L = 1024); t = 10^9 in about 0.6 ms (L = 1024).
new.title: Fuse fast-forward by burn times

new.improvement_detail: exact and generic; useless when transients or periods are long (affine quasigroups, many geometric-width rules); memory grows with mu + lambda
new.novelty_basis: Cycle detection (Floyd, Brent) is classical.
new.statement: Storing visited rows answers a query t in mu + lambda simulated steps; for random rows of length 32 this is at most 5000 steps for 1590 of 1734 order-3 classes (median transient 5, median period 2), but it fails for the affine quasigroups and for 128 of 300 geometric-width classes.
new.title: Cycle detection as a generic fast-forward

new.limitations: Laver tables only for t <= 8 (A_2) and t <= 5 (A_3).
new.statement: The Laver tables A_2 and A_3 give automata whose light cones depend on at most 3 resp. 4 cells (t <= 8 resp. 5) with widths 4 and 8; GF(4) multiplication and XOR on [0,4) have width 4; the anchored golden- and odd-law models of C06 are permutive (hence surjective) affine automata.
new.title: Earlier structures of the lab as automata

new.limitations: True for affine magmas and commutative semigroups (Theorems 2-3); no algorithm is known for the 685 bounded-width order-3 classes outside the structured classes, and bounded width does not give short cycles (the affine quasigroups have long ones).
new.statement: Every magma automaton with bounded streaming width admits an algorithm computing a cyclic row of length L at time t in time polynomial in L and log t.
new.title: Bounded streaming width implies a fast-forward

new: The 16 two-element magma automata c'_i = c_i * c_{i+1} are exactly the elementary rules 17m (rules ignoring the left neighbour). XOR (rule 102) has 2^popcount(t) essential cells (Gould's sequence). All 16 have streaming width <= 3 up to t = 18; NAND (rule 119) depends on at most 3 cells. Surjective - rules 51, 85, 102, 153, 170, 204; injective - 51, 85, 170, 204.

1734 order-3 classes (3330 up to isomorphism; 19683 tables). Streaming-width classes on t <= 9 - bounded 808, linear 104, geometric 300, other 522. All 18 semigroup and 8 affine classes are bounded (width <= 3), but 685 bounded-width classes lie outside semigroups, affine magmas and bounded dependence (only 163 of the 808 are explained by these or by an associative/affine eventual image). 43 classes (420 tables) are surjective, exactly the permutive ones; 7 are injective (reversible), including two whose light cones use all t+1 cells; 34 are nilpotent by t = 9.
linear width growth, e.g. the fuse magma [[0,0,0],[0,0,1],[1,2,2]] with lambda(t) = t + 2 (H-C15-1)
bounded width outside the predicted classes, e.g. the reversible automaton [[0,0,2],[2,2,0],[1,1,1]] (full light cone, width 3, neither associative nor affine) (H-C15-2)

99/99 fast-forward results agree with direct simulation (9 magmas, L in {256, 1024, 4096}, t up to 10^5). Indicative speedups at L = 1024 - affine magmas x3-4 at t = 100, x22-29 at 10^3, x138-215 at 10^4, x1800-2500 at 10^5, t = 10^9 in 1.5-8 ms (L <= 4096); fuse x2.5 at t = 100 and about x4000 at 10^5; commutative semigroups only x62-100 at 10^5 and slower than simulation (x0.5-0.9) around t = 10^3 for L >= 1024, because of the O(L^2) product step.
H-C15-6: the commutative-semigroup method stays below x100 at L = 1024, t = 10^5 (mult mod 3 x62, min x77); the affine and fuse methods never lose to simulation, even at t = 100

Cycle detection on one random cyclic row per order-3 class - L = 16 1693/1734, L = 32 1590/1734, L = 64 1561/1734 rows repeat within 5000 steps (median transient 4-6, median period 2). All bounded- and linear-width classes repeat quickly except the four affine Z_3 quasigroups (x + y and relatives), which have bounded width but long cycles; geometric-width classes often do not repeat (172/300 at L = 32).
H-C15-5: the bounded-width affine quasigroup x*y = x + y (mod 3) does not repeat within 5000 steps at L = 32 and 64

The fuse magma has lambda(t) = t + 2 for t = 1..12 and the residual family of the lower-bound proof separates as predicted. Laver tables A_2, A_3 - bounded dependence (3 resp. 4 cells) and widths 4 resp. 8, not surjective. GF(4) multiplication and XOR on [0,4) - widths 4. Anchored affine models of C06 (golden law N = 5, 11; odd law N = 5) - permutive, hence surjective, and affine-fast-forwardable. The order-4 rectangular band is surjective and injective but not permutive. OEIS - essential cells of x + y mod 3 = A006047; the count 1, 6, 420 of surjective tables matches only the unrelated A273820 (lcm of 2^n..2^(n+1)-1, a three-term coincidence); the geometric width sequence 3, 3, 6, 9, 19, 42, 88, ... has no match.

new.novelty_basis: S. Markovski, D. Gligoroski, V. Bakeva, Quasigroup string processing, Part 1, Contributions, Sec. Math. Tech. Sci., MANU (1999) - the E- and D-transformations with the same leader are mutually inverse permutations of strings (as cited in US patent 8041031, https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8041031, and in Markovski-Bakeva, Quasigroup String Processing Part 4, https://www.academia.edu/115482463/Quasigroup_String_Processing_Part_4).
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (eT_injective, eT_length; standard axioms only) plus the finite-cardinality step (written proof, proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 1); d(e(X)) = X for all seven quasigroups (EXP-C18-01)
new.statement: For every quasigroup Q, leader l and length n, the e-transformation e_l is a bijection of Q^n, inverted by the d-transformation a_i = b_(i-1) \ b_i; hence every composition of forward and reversed e-transformations is a bijection of Q^n.
new.title: e-transformations are bijections of strings of fixed length

new.novelty_basis: Elementary; implicit in the quasigroup-string-processing literature.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the persistence of differences (eT_ne_of_ne; standard axioms only); agreement before i and the corollary by written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 2); 0 violations on 7 x 2000 random strings (EXP-C18-01); max bias 0.5 for all three forward-only variants (EXP-C18-02)
new.statement: If u and v differ exactly at position i, then e_l(u) and e_l(v) agree at positions < i and differ at every position >= i. Consequently, in a hash that outputs the last 8 bytes of forward e-transformations only, changing a message byte at position i >= n - 8 leaves the earlier tail bytes unchanged, so some output bits never flip and the maximal avalanche bias is 1/2.
new.title: Differences propagate forward only; forward-only tail hashes fail the strict avalanche criterion

new.novelty_basis: An elementary narrow-pipe property of byte-level e-transformations. Quasigroup hash designs submitted to the SHA-3 competition used huge quasigroups in wide-pipe constructions (Edon-R, orders 2^256-2^512, https://ehash.isec.tugraz.at/uploads/7/74/Edon.pdf; NaSHA, https://eprint.iacr.org/2008/519), which avoids it; two searches found no explicit statement of the bound for byte-level e-transformation hashes.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the factorisation of the tail through one state (eT_append, eT_tail_factors) and injectivity (eT_injective); the counting consequences by written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 3); the bound is attained exactly (256 values) in 100 families of 4096 keys (EXP-C18-05) and explains the 32,624 full collisions of EXP-C18-03 exactly
new.statement:
The last k outputs of an e-transformation are a bijective function of the state before them and the last k
inputs. Hence a hash outputting the last 8 bytes after p forward e-transformations takes at most 256^p values on
messages sharing their last 7 bytes, and with a final reversed e-transformation it takes at most 256 values on
messages sharing their first 7 bytes, for every p and every quasigroup of order 256.
new.title: The tail-information bound: an e-transformation tail carries one byte of state

new.novelty_basis: Closure of T-functions under composition - A. Klimov, A. Shamir, A new class of invertible mappings, CHES 2002; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-function and https://www.iacr.org/archive/fse2004/30170001/30170001.pdf.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 4, induction along the chains using x = x' and y = y' mod 2^r => x*y = x'*y' mod 2^r); 0 low-bit changes for AFF, XOR, ALP in EXP-C18-01; max bias 0.5 in EXP-C18-02
new.statement: If x*y is a T-function on Z/2^8, then in every QG hash (any number of forward and reversed e-transformations) bit j of every output byte depends only on bits 0..j of the message bytes; flipping an input bit at position r never changes an output bit at a position < r, and the maximal avalanche bias is 1/2.
new.title: T-function quasigroups (affine mod 256, XOR, (x + 1) XOR y) cannot mix high input bits into low output bits

new.novelty_basis: Folklore (affine maps compose to affine maps; the same property makes CRCs unsuitable as hash-table mixers).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 5); one distinct output difference over 2000 keys (EXP-C18-01); mean bias 0.5 for QG-XOR and for CRC32 (EXP-C18-02)
new.statement: If x*y = A(x) XOR B(y) XOR c with A, B linear over GF(2) (for example x XOR y), every QG hash satisfies H(M XOR D) = H(M) XOR L(D) for a fixed linear L; every avalanche cell is 0 or 1.
new.title: GF(2)-affine quasigroups give GF(2)-affine hashes with key-independent differences

new.novelty_basis: Elementary; shows that an anchored quasigroup of C06 (Theorem 4 there) is a poor mixing primitive.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 6); 2000/2000 one-pass hashes unchanged under prefix permutations (EXP-C18-01); bit independence 1.0 with ideal per-bit flip rates for QG-ARP p2+rev (EXP-C18-02); 36,720 full collisions for QG-ARP p1 on near-duplicates (EXP-C18-03)
new.statement: For x*y = x + c(y) mod 256, two runs over the same inputs from states b, b' differ by the constant b' - b at every position, and one pass computes prefix sums l + sum c(a_i). Hence the one-pass tail hash is unchanged by permutations of the message bytes before the tail, and with a reverse pass all 8 output bytes change by one common additive constant when a message byte at position >= 8 changes (perfectly correlated bit changes).
new.title: The anchored quasigroup x + c(y): additive differences persist, and the one-pass hash is anagram-blind

new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C18.md Theorem 7, triangular composition of row and column bijections); quality of the cascades measured separately (EXP-C18-05)
new.statement: In the cascade QC(T, d) (d e-transformations run in parallel, output = the final state of every pass), the update of the state (s_1, ..., s_d) by one input byte is a bijection of Q^d; so states are never merged and the tail-information bound does not apply to the output.
new.title: The 8-pass cascade has a bijective 64-bit state update

new.limitations: Holds (0.0089 / 0.041 versus 0.0089 / 0.045, also with one forward pass), but the same hash fails every structured distribution test (CLM-C18-03) - single-bit avalanche statistics cannot see the tail-information bound.
new.statement: QG-LS p2+rev has mean and maximal avalanche bias within 0.01 of BLAKE2b-64 on 2000 random 16-byte keys.
new.title: H-C18-1: QG-LS with 2 passes and a reverse pass has BLAKE2b-level avalanche

new.limitations: Proved (bias 1/2) for the T-function and GF(2)-affine quasigroups (CLM-C18-04, CLM-C18-05). For x + c(y) with a reverse pass the difference (0.043 versus 0.041) is within sampling noise; its defect shows in bit independence instead (CLM-C18-06), which the hypothesis did not measure.
new.statement: Every structured quasigroup tested (affine, XOR, x + c(y), (x + 1) XOR y) gives a larger maximal avalanche bias than the random Latin square in the same construction.
new.title: H-C18-2: structured quasigroups are worse mixers than a random Latin square (maximal avalanche bias)

new.counterexample: Avalanche is better than FNV-1a's (max bias 0.0415 vs 0.5), but on the decimal strings 0..65535 the 1024-bucket z-score is 1084 and the bucket-collision ratio 2.62, and near-duplicate keys give 32,624 full 64-bit collisions (FNV-1a: z = -9.8, ratio 0.995, 0 full collisions) - the tail-information bound (CLM-C18-03).
new.statement: QG-NIMINV p2+rev (x*y = (x XOR y)^-1 in the nimber field of order 256) has avalanche at least as good as FNV-1a-64 and, like FNV-1a, |chi-square z| <= 3 and a bucket-collision ratio within 2% on all four key sets.
new.title: H-C18-3: the nimber-field quasigroup gives a hash competitive with FNV-1a (refuted)

new.counterexample: QC-NIMINV d8 - maximal avalanche bias 0.0845 against 0.045 for BLAKE2b (about 7 standard deviations of a cell) and z = -3.21 (1021 buckets) on synthetic words; QC-LS d8 and QC-ISO d8 pass every test (EXP-C18-05).
new.statement: The cascades QC-LS, QC-ISO and QC-NIMINV (depth 8, 8 zero bytes of finalisation) have avalanche within 0.01 of BLAKE2b-64, |z| <= 3, collision ratios within 2% and no full collisions on all four key sets.
new.title: H-C18-8: the 8-pass cascade over LS, ISO and NIMINV passes every test (refuted)

new.counterexample: QC-ARP d8 has maximal correlation 0.176 (noise level about 0.11) - the cascade removes the perfect correlation of QG-ARP p2+rev, although 5 avalanche cells still exceed bias 0.1 (EXP-C18-05).
new.statement: The cascade QC-ARP d8 has a maximal bit-independence correlation of at least 0.5.
new.title: H-C18-9: the cascade over x + c(y) still fails bit independence (refuted)

new.improvement_detail: Every tail-output variant fails at least one quality test (forward-only - avalanche; reverse-pass - distribution, 2.4-2.7x bucket collisions and 32,624 full collisions on near-duplicates). The cascades over the random Latin square and the Z/256 isotope match MX64 and BLAKE2b-64 on every quality test run, but at 10-13 MB/s they were about 3x slower than BLAKE2b (one C call per key) and over 10x slower than numpy-vectorised MX64 in the same run (EXP-C18-05; EXP-C18-04 under different load - FNV-1a 640, MX64 428, BLAKE2b 74 MB/s, quasigroup variants 11-52 MB/s). MX64 is at least as good on every axis. Against FNV-1a alone, the good cascades have better avalanche (FNV-1a max bias 0.5) and better distribution on sequential keys (FNV-1a z = -9.8), at a large speed cost. This is not a security evaluation.
new.limitations: Python/numpy implementations on a shared machine (times indicative); a small subset of SMHasher-style tests; one random Latin square (not uniformly sampled); 16-byte keys for avalanche.
new.novelty_basis: Quasigroup string processing for cryptographic primitives and pseudo-random generators is established (Markovski et al.; Gligoroski, Candidate one-way functions and one-way permutations based on quasigroup string transformations, https://ia.cr/2005/352; Edon-R); the benchmark against these baselines is ours.
new.statement: Among 13 tail-output quasigroup hashes and 4 cascades, measured against FNV-1a-64, MX64 (multiply-xorshift with the splitmix64 finaliser), BLAKE2b-64 and CRC32 on avalanche, bit independence, chi-square, collisions and throughput, no quasigroup construction improves on the best baseline in any measured dimension.
new.title: Quasigroup hashes against non-cryptographic baselines - no improvement

new: Seven tables of order 256 are quasigroups - a random Latin square (row-by-row random matchings, not uniform), a random isotope of Z/256, the nimber inversion quasigroup (x XOR y)^-1, affine 77x + 141y + 5, XOR, and the anchored x + c(y) and (x + 1) XOR y of C06. AFF, XOR and ALP are T-functions; only XOR is GF(2)-affine. The nim-product is not a quasigroup on [0,256) (row 0 is zero); its nonzero part is a group; nim_mul agrees with the C07 mex table on [0,64). All predictions of Theorems 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 hold on random inputs: d(e(X)) = X, 0 single-difference violations, 0 low-bit changes for the T-function quasigroups, one key-independent output difference for XOR, 2000 of 2000 one-pass x + c(y) hashes unchanged under prefix permutations.

Avalanche and bit independence on 2000 random 16-byte keys. At the BLAKE2b-64 noise floor (mean bias 0.0089, max 0.045, BIC 0.11) - QG-LS with a reverse pass (1, 2 or 4 forward passes), QG-ISO p2+rev, QG-NIMINV p1/p2+rev, MX64. QG-ARP p2+rev also has ideal per-bit flip rates (max bias 0.043) but perfectly correlated bit changes (BIC 1.0). Failing - every forward-only variant (max bias 0.5, mean 0.09-0.10), FNV-1a-64 (mean 0.098, max 0.5, 1688 cells above 0.1), the T-function quasigroups AFF and ALP (mean 0.39 and 0.34) and the GF(2)-affine XOR and CRC32 (mean 0.5).

Distribution on four key sets of about 65,536 keys (random strings, decimal 0..65535, near-duplicates, synthetic words). Every reverse-pass QG variant fails on the three structured sets (chi-square z up to 26,000 with 1024 buckets, 2.4-2.7 times the expected bucket collisions, 32,624 full 64-bit collisions on near-duplicates) - exactly as the tail-information bound predicts; the 2-pass forward hash passes the chi-square tests but has 723 full collisions on near-duplicates. MX64 and BLAKE2b pass everything; FNV-1a and CRC32 fail mildly on sequential and near-duplicate keys (z = -9.8 and -20.5 for sequential keys). A first run failed (synthetic words passed as str instead of bytes) and was fixed; the corrected META key count (65,280 near-duplicates) reproduced the same result hash.
QG-NIMINV p2+rev: z = 1084 (1024 buckets) on the decimal strings 0..65535 and 32,624 full 64-bit collisions on near-duplicate keys (H-C18-3 refuted)

Throughput for 16,384 keys of 64 bytes (indicative, shared machine at load 5-6) - FNV-1a 640 MB/s and MX64 428 MB/s (numpy, vectorised over keys), CRC32 127 MB/s and BLAKE2b 74 MB/s (C library, one call per key), quasigroup variants 11-52 MB/s. Every reverse-pass quasigroup variant was slower than FNV-1a on 8- and 64-byte keys (H-C18-4).

The tail-information bound holds exactly on data - 256 distinct hash values in each of 50 families of 4096 keys sharing a 7-byte prefix (reverse-pass hash) or the last 7 message bytes (one-pass forward hash). The 8-pass cascade QC (output = final state of every pass) over the random Latin square and over the Z/256 isotope is at the BLAKE2b noise floor on avalanche and bit independence and passes all distribution and collision tests; over the nimber inversion quasigroup it shows a real bias (max 0.0845) and one marginal chi-square flag (z = -3.21 on words); over x + c(y) the bit-independence defect drops from 1.0 to 0.176 but 5 avalanche cells exceed 0.1. Cascade throughput about 10-13 MB/s versus MX64 165 MB/s and BLAKE2b 41 MB/s in the same run.
QC-NIMINV d8: maximal avalanche bias 0.0845 (BLAKE2b 0.045) and z = -3.21 (1021 buckets) on synthetic words (H-C18-8 refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Every function M x M -> M is the feedback of a unique magma, so pair maps are exactly the order-2 feedback shift registers over n letters, and the criterion is the q-ary form of Golomb's nonsingularity condition (S. W. Golomb, Shift Register Sequences, 1967; see e.g. arXiv:1911.06670 for the binary statement and the correspondence of nonsingular registers with factors of the de Bruijn graph).
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib (pairMap_injective_iff, pairMap_bijective_iff, mirrorMap_eq; standard axioms only); count by written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 1) and exhaustive check n <= 4 (EXP-C16-01)
new.statement:
For a finite magma (M, *), the pair map P(a, b) = (b, b*a) of the recurrence x_{k+1} = x_k * x_{k-1} is a
bijection iff every left translation a -> b*a is a bijection; hence exactly (n!)^n of the n^(n^2) tables of
order n give permutations. The mirror recurrence x_{k+1} = x_{k-1} * x_k is the forward recurrence of the
opposite magma.
new.title: The Fibonacci pair map of a magma is a permutation iff every left translation is a bijection

new.counterexample: x*y = 1 - y on {0,1} has the single cycle (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (1,1) -> (1,0) of length 4 = n^2 and is not a quasigroup; every n has full-period tables (Theorem 2); for n <= 4 none of them is a quasigroup (EXP-C16-01).
new.statement: As for Pisano periods (where (0, 0) is fixed), the maximal period of the pair map on an n-element magma is at most n^2 - 1, and the maximum is attained only by quasigroups.
new.title: H-C16-1: maximal period at most n^2 - 1, attained only by quasigroups (refuted)

new.novelty_basis: Translation of a classical fact - the number of de Bruijn sequences B(k, m) is (k!)^(k^(m-1)) / k^m (T. van Aardenne-Ehrenfest, N. G. de Bruijn, Simon Stevin 28 (1951); BEST theorem; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Bruijn_sequence).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 2) using the van Aardenne-Ehrenfest--de Bruijn count; exhaustive confirmation for n = 2, 3, 4 (EXP-C16-01); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
A table of order n is full-period (its pair map is one cycle through all n^2 states) iff the symbol sequence
along that cycle is a de Bruijn cycle of order 2 over n symbols, and this is a bijection; hence there are exactly
(n!)^n / n^2 full-period tables of order n (1, 24, 20736, ...) and the maximal period over n-element magmas is
n^2 for every n >= 1.
new.title: Full-period magmas are de Bruijn cycles: there are (n!)^n / n^2 of them

new.novelty_basis: Elementary; likely known in the shift-register literature in other forms (Golomb's cycle-parity results for binary registers); no search for the q-ary order-2 statement beyond two web searches.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 3, factorisation P = swap o fibrewise translations); satisfied by every full-period table found (EXP-C16-01/02); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement: If every left translation L_b is a bijection, sign(P) = (-1)^(n(n-1)/2) prod_b sgn(L_b); hence a full-period table satisfies prod_b sgn(L_b) = (-1)^((n-1)(n+2)/2).
new.title: A parity condition for full periods

new.novelty_basis: Searched (2026-10-18) - de Bruijn cycles with distance constraints, universal cycles of Latin squares/quasigroups, Tuscan-2 squares (Etzion, Golomb, Taylor, Adv. Appl. Math. 10 (1989) - a related but different object: n x n arrays, pairs at distance <= 2 at most once across rows), orthogonal de Bruijn sequences. No statement of this characterisation or of these cycles found. Small.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 4); the exhaustive Latin-square count and the independent distance-1/2 DFS count agree (EXP-C16-02); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
A full-period table is a quasigroup iff in its cycle x_0 ... x_{n^2-1} every ordered pair also occurs exactly once
as (x_i, x_{i+2}); equivalently the windows (x_{i-1}, x_i, x_{i+1}) run once through the n^2 triples
(a, b, b*a) of the Latin square (a universal cycle of the quasigroup).
new.title: Full-period quasigroups are cycles in which every pair occurs once at distance 1 and once at distance 2

new.counterexample: True for n = 2, 3, 4, false for n = 5 - exactly 3360 of the 161280 Latin squares of order 5 are full-period (e.g. the cycle 0,0,1,0,2,2,0,3,3,1,2,1,4,0,4,4,2,3,2,4,1,1,3,4,3); examples exist for every order 6-16 (EXP-C16-02).
new.statement: For every n, no quasigroup of order n has a full-period pair map; the maximal period of a quasigroup of order n is n^2 - 1.
new.title: H-C16-5: no quasigroup has a full-period pair map (refuted)

new.statement:
There is no full-period quasigroup of order 2, 3 or 4; there are exactly 3360 of order 5, forming 28 isomorphism
classes; full-period quasigroups of every order 6, ..., 16 and of orders 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 56, 63, 72 exist.

new.statement: If two magmas (or quasigroups) of coprime orders n1, n2 are full-period, so is their direct product (a quasigroup if both are).
new.title: Direct products of full-period magmas of coprime orders are full-period

Soc. Bull. 56 (2005) - study generating pairs, not full periods). Small.

new.statement: For every group G of even order n = 2m and every isotope x o y = gamma(alpha(x) beta(y)), prod_b sgn(L_b) = (-1)^m, whereas a full period requires (-1)^(m+1); so no group of even order and no isotope of one is full-period. (For odd n isotopes of Z_n are full-period for every n = 5, ..., 15.)
new.title: No isotope of a group of even order has a full-period Fibonacci pair map

new.limitations: Verified for n = 5..16 and for the products 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 56, 63, 72; sampling hit rates (about 1/n^2 per random Latin square of the right parity) suggest the number of full-period quasigroups grows like L(n)/n^2, but there is no proof. Plain depth-first search and a SAT encoding stall at n = 9, so random sampling was the only method that scaled.
new.statement: For every n >= 5 there is a quasigroup of order n whose Fibonacci pair map is a single cycle through all n^2 pairs.
new.title: Full-period quasigroups exist for every order n >= 5

new.statement: P(a, b) = (a, b) iff a = b and a*a = a; an idempotent magma has n fixed points and maximal period at most n^2 - n, so no idempotent quasigroup is full-period.
new.title: Fixed points of the pair map are idempotents

new.novelty_basis: Periods of second-order linear recurrences modulo N are orders of companion matrices (M. Ward, Trans. AMS 35 (1933); D. D. Wall, Amer. Math. Monthly 67 (1960) for Fibonacci). The resulting period sequences of the odd and golden laws (6, 24, 48, 18, 5, ... and 4, 120, 342, ...) are not in the OEIS.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 9, conjugation to the linear map and a cyclic vector); Lean for the anchored conjugacy (anchored_fibonacci); exhaustive confirmation for anchored N <= 60, odd N <= 61 and 51 golden pairs (EXP-C16-03)
new.statement:
For x*y = alpha x + beta y + gamma on Z/N (beta a unit) whose pair map has a fixed point, the maximal period is the
order of [[0,1],[beta,alpha]] mod N. In particular the anchored associative magma x + y + 1 has exactly the cycle
structure of the Fibonacci numbers mod N (maximal period = the Pisano period), the odd-law magma x + 1 + y/2 has
maximal period ord([[0,1],[1/2,1]]) and the golden-law magmas x + 1 + a y (a^2 + a = 1) have maximal period
ord([[0,1],[a,1]]).
new.title: Affine magmas: periods are orders of companion matrices; the anchored magma x + y + 1 is the Fibonacci sequence mod N

new.limitations: 300 of 300 random cases with N <= 30. Proven only when the pair map has a fixed point (CLM-C16-12) - in general the matrix order is the lcm of all orbit lengths, and equality with the maximum needs a vector whose orbit attains the lcm.
new.statement: For every affine magma x*y = alpha x + beta y + gamma on Z/N with beta a unit, the maximal period of the pair map equals the order of [[0,1,0],[beta,alpha,gamma],[0,0,1]] mod N.
new.title: For affine magmas the maximal period equals the order of the 3x3 affine matrix

new.novelty_basis: The Fibonacci length of a cyclic group is its Pisano period (classical; Knox 1992, Campbell et al.); nimber fields are Conway's.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C16.md Theorem 10, discrete logarithms in the field of nimbers); confirmed for q = 16, 256 (EXP-C16-03)
new.statement: On [0, q), q = 2^(2^k), with nim-multiplication the pair map sends pairs containing 0 to (0, 0) within two steps and is isomorphic on nonzero pairs to the Fibonacci pair map on (Z/(q-1))^2; its maximal period is pi(q - 1) (40 for q = 16, 360 for q = 256).
new.title: Fibonacci sequences of nimbers: maximal period pi(2^(2^k) - 1)

new.novelty_basis: No source connecting Fibonacci-type recurrences with Laver tables was found (web search 2026-10-18; Laver-table surveys arXiv:1810.00548, Wikipedia). An easy consequence of Laver's monotonicity; small.

new.statement:
For n >= 1 and N = 2^n, the pair map of the Laver table A_n (0-based) has exactly N cycles - the fixed point
(N-1, N-1) and the two-cycles {(N-1, c), (c, N-1)} - and every orbit reaches one of them; so the maximal period is 2
(H-C16-4, 'the maximal period is a power of 2', holds for this degenerate reason).
new.title: Laver tables: every Fibonacci orbit ends in the fixed point or one of the N - 1 two-cycles through the top element

new.limitations: No explanation; the proof of CLM-C16-15 only gives the bound N.
new.statement: The longest transient of the Laver pair map (steps until the state contains the top element) is 1, 3, 3 for n = 1, 2, 3 and exactly 5 for every n = 4, ..., 10.
new.title: Fibonacci orbits in Laver tables reach the top element within 5 steps (n <= 10)

new.improvement_detail: every magma generator fails at least two tests that PCG64 passes; the longest periods available to order-2 recurrences (n^2 symbols) are far too short for practical use, and affine generators inherit the known low-bit weaknesses of lagged Fibonacci/multiple recursive generators

new.novelty_basis: Low-bit periodicity of additive generators modulo 2^w and the non-uniformity of Fibonacci numbers modulo 2^k are classical (Knuth, TAOCP vol. 2, 3.2.2; H. Niederreiter, Fibonacci Quart. 10 (1972) - uniform distribution only modulo powers of 5).
new.statement: On a simple battery (byte chi-square, serial pairs, lowest-bit period, lag-1 correlation; 2^20 outputs) the anchored Fibonacci and affine magma generators on Z/2^32 fail low-byte uniformity and have lowest-bit period 3, and the de Bruijn byte magma (maximal possible period 65536) is too regular; PCG64 passes every test.
new.title: Magma Fibonacci generators are not competitive pseudo-random generators

new.statement:
For any finite set E of laws, the anchored affine tables are exactly x*y = x + a*y + 1, and the affine spectrum
Aff(E) is the set of N for which the affine system of E (polynomials in Z[a]) has a common root mod N. Aff(E) is
closed under divisors and under coprime products; if the system has no common factor over Q it is finite and
equal to the set of divisors of its maximum L (which divides a resultant of the system), and otherwise it is
infinite.

new.statement: For every term V(y, z) not containing x, every anchored model of (x*y)*z = x*V(y, z) is a translation table x*y = x + 1 + k(y) with k a permutation of Z/N fixing 0, and k satisfies k(V(y,z)) = k(y) + k(z) + 1.
new.title: Right-normed laws (xy)z = x V(y,z) have only translation models

new.novelty_basis: Searched (2026-10-18) - anchored/successor-anchored magmas (only Laver tables), spectra of varieties (Taylor 1980; Kearnes), roots of the tribonacci polynomial mod p (Klaska-Skula, Fibonacci Quart. 2010; Moree-Noubissie arXiv:2205.06685); no correspondence between magma laws and n-bonacci congruences found. The number theory of the resulting sets is classical.
new.proof_check: Lean 4 + Mathlib for the model correspondence for every W (w_family_models, w_family_model_of_root, linear_of_shift, T1.eval_affine, T1.cpoly_eq; standard axioms only); the characterisation of the occurring c_W by written proof (proofs/paper/C13.md Theorem 3 (iv)); 0 mismatches on 23 terms for N <= 9 (EXP-C13-03)
new.statement:
For every one-variable term W(z), the anchored models of (x*y)*z = x*(y*W(z)) are exactly the affine tables
x*y = x + 1 + a*y with a*c_W(a) = 1 (mod N), c_W(a) the sum over the leaves of W of a^(number of right steps);
distinct roots give distinct models. The occurring polynomials c_W are exactly those with non-negative integer
coefficients, constant term 1 and no gaps. In particular the right comb with n leaves gives the spectrum of the
n-bonacci polynomial (golden law for n = 2, tribonacci law for n = 3) and the left comb with k + 1 leaves the
condition k*a^2 + a - 1 = 0.
new.title: The W-family: anchored models of (xy)z = x(y W(z)) are the affine tables with a*c_W(a) = 1

new.novelty_basis: Settles two cases of the lab's own conjecture CLM-C06-10; no prior statement expected or found. Small.

new.statement: The law x(yz) = ((zx)x)y has anchored models exactly for N in {1, 3} (unique model x*y = x + 1 + 2y at N = 3), and x(yz) = ((xy)z)x exactly for N in {1, 2} (unique model x*y = x + 1 at N = 2).
new.title: Exact finite spectra {1,3} and {1,2} for x(yz) = ((zx)x)y and x(yz) = ((xy)z)x

new.statement: The one-variable law x = x*(x*(x*x)) has an anchored model of every size N != 2 and none of size 2; in particular its spectrum contains 4 but not 2, so anchored spectra need not be closed under divisors.
new.title: The law x = x(x(xx)) has anchored models of every size except 2

new.novelty_basis: Congruence closure with integer offsets is a standard decision-procedure idea (difference/offset equalities, Nelson-Oppen style); its use as a spectrum prover for anchored magmas is the lab's.
new.proof_check: written soundness proof (proofs/paper/C13.md Theorem 6); applications computer-assisted (Python, EXP-C13-08) - trust base is the closure code, cross-checked against SAT/affine models on 603 laws (235 with a bound, 1,245 sizes) with 0 contradictions; awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
The procedure offset_closure_bound (systems/anchored.py) returns g >= 0 such that N | g for every anchored model of
size N. If g > 0 and every divisor of g admits an affine model, the anchored spectrum is exactly Div(g). This proves
the conjectured spectra {1,3} resp. {1,2} of CLM-C06-10 for all its laws except x(yz) = y((yx)z), and the exact
finite spectrum Div(g) for 6,912 of the 18,581 laws over {x,y,z} with <= 4 leaves per side (6,045 of them have
only the trivial model).
new.title: Offset congruence closure is a sound prover of finite anchored spectra; it settles 16 of the 17 laws of CLM-C06-10

new.counterexample: x = x(x(xx)) has models of every size except 2 (CLM-C13-05, Lean). Violations are common - 24 of 253 one-variable laws (N <= 12), 81 of 300 random 2-variable laws (N <= 9), 29 of 150 random 3-variable laws and 17 of 80 random pairs of laws (N <= 8); e.g. ((xy)x)y = (y(xx))x has models at N = 6 and 8 but none at N = 2, 3, 4, 5.
new.statement: If a set of laws has an anchored model of size N, it has one of every size d dividing N.
new.title: H-C13-1: every anchored spectrum is closed under divisors (refuted)

new.counterexample: 198 of the 199 laws tested have non-affine models (EXP-C13-02), e.g. x = x(x(xx)) (affine spectrum A034017, non-affine models for N = 3..8) and (xx)x = (yy)y (non-affine models for N = 2..8).
new.statement: For every law with at most 4 leaves per side (3 variables) or 5 leaves per side (2 variables) whose affine spectrum is infinite and not all N, every anchored model is affine.
new.title: H-C13-2: laws with an infinite non-trivial affine spectrum are affinely rigid (refuted)

new.counterexample: x = (xx)x has spectrum exactly {1, 2}: at x = 0 the anchor gives 0 = 2, and x*y = x + 1 is a model of size 2; likewise x = ((xx)x)x has spectrum {1, 3} and x = (((xx)x)x)x has {1, 2, 4} (proofs/paper/C13.md, remark after Theorem 5).
new.statement: Every law t1(x) = t2(x) in one variable has anchored spectrum {1} or contains all sufficiently large N.
new.title: H-C13-5: a one-variable law has spectrum {1} or a cofinite spectrum (refuted)
