new.statement: Every one-variable law t1(x) = t2(x) has an anchored spectrum that is either finite or contains all sufficiently large N.
new.title: Spectra of one-variable laws are finite or cofinite

new.novelty_basis: The sets are classical (OEIS entries quoted). Their realisation as affine anchored spectra of single magma laws was not found (searches as for CLM-C13-03). These are affine spectra only - by EXP-C13-02 the true spectra of the short laws realising them are usually larger; true spectra are realised for the W-family sets (CLM-C13-03).
new.proof_check: affine systems computed mechanically (EXP-C13-01) and Theorem 1 (written); the identification of each root set with the stated arithmetic condition is elementary (e.g. a^2 - 2a - 1 = 0 iff (a - 1)^2 = 2); terms <= 200 agree with the OEIS entries A005408, A001651, A008784, A057126, A057125, A034017, A089270, A004613, A058529, A192453, A354467
new.statement:
The affine anchored spectrum of a law is {N : the gcd of its affine system has a root mod N} (up to the finitely many
exceptional primes of Theorem 1). Among laws with at most 4 leaves (3 variables) or 5 leaves (2 variables) this
realises - via the polynomials 2a + 1, 3a + 1, a^2 + 1, a^2 - 2a - 1, a^2 + 2a - 2, a^2 + a + 1, a^2 - a - 1,
2a^2 + 2a + 1, 2a^2 - 1, a^4 + 1, a^4 - a^2 + 1 - the odd numbers, the numbers prime to 3, and the numbers N
modulo which -1, 2, 3 are squares, x^2 + x + 1 has a root, the golden ratio exists, all prime factors are 1 mod 4,
+-1 mod 8 or 1 mod 12, and -1 is a fourth power (e.g. x(xx) = y(xy) for -1 a square, (xx)(xy) = (yy)(yx) for 2
a square).
new.title: Single laws whose affine spectra are classical arithmetic sets

new.limitations: Sizes N <= 8-9 only; a sparse infinite spectrum cannot be recognised from so few sizes. Question 3 of the cycle remains open.
new.statement: Among the 198 non-rigid laws of EXP-C13-02, 190 have anchored models at every N = 6, 7, 8 (the others have UNKNOWN instances or small exceptions); no law other than left-distributivity was found whose non-affine models occur only at sparse sizes such as powers of two.
new.title: Non-affine models typically exist for all sizes beyond a small threshold; no Laver-like sparse spectrum found

new: Affine atlas. The 18,581 laws over {x,y,z} with <= 4 leaves per side fall into 2,400 affine systems and 27 distinct affine spectra; the 75,625 laws over {x,y} with <= 5 leaves per side into 3,631 systems and 125 spectra. Every finite affine spectrum is a divisor set Div(L) (80 values of L up to 328). The infinite ones are classical number-theoretic sets, identified by OEIS - odd numbers (A005408), 3 does not divide N (A001651), -1 is a square (A008784), 2 is a square (A057126), 3 is a square (A057125), x^2+xy+y^2 (A034017), golden (A089270), prime factors 1 mod 4 (A004613), prime factors +-1 mod 8 (A058529), -1 a fourth power (A192453), prime factors 1 mod 12 (A354467), forms of discriminant -7, -11, 13 (A244779, A244780, A243656) and -8-type (A225771); about thirty cubic and quartic conditions (plastic number x^3 - x - 1, tribonacci, tetranacci, 5th cyclotomic polynomial, ...) give sequences with no OEIS match.

Rigidity test - the 3 shortest laws of every infinite non-trivial affine class (199 laws), all affine tables blocked, N = 2..8. 198 laws have non-affine anchored models (most at every N from 3 to 8); only x((yz)z) = z((yx)x) is rigid on the tested range; 12 UNKNOWN instances (N = 7, 8). H-C13-2 refuted. 190 of the 198 non-rigid laws have models at every N = 6, 7, 8. The short laws of each class are weak (e.g. x = x(x(xx)) constrains only diagonals). A first run with 4 laws per class, N <= 9 and budget 2,000,000 was stopped after 17 CPU-minutes.
x = x(x(xx)): affine spectrum A034017 (1, 3, 7, 13, ...) but non-affine anchored models for N = 3..8

Theorem 3 (W-family) tested before it was proved - for all 23 one-variable terms W with <= 5 leaves and N = 1..9, the anchored models of (xy)z = x(y W(z)) are exactly the affine tables with a*c_W(a) = 1: 0 mismatches. 16 distinct polynomials c_W occur; the golden law gives A089270, c_W = 1 + 3a gives A243656, c_W = 1 + a + 2a^2 gives the odd numbers, and the tribonacci and tetranacci laws give spectra not in the OEIS.

The 17 laws of CLM-C06-10, N = 2..12, one SAT call per size with all affine tables blocked - every spectrum agrees with the conjectured set {1,3} or {1,2}; the only non-affine model is the known one of x(yz) = y((yx)z) at N = 2; 0 UNKNOWN.

Divisor-closure, 300 random 2-variable laws (<= 4 leaves per side), N <= 9 with pruning - 251 laws have a model of some size 2..9 and 81 violate divisor-closure; violating pairs (N, d) - (8,2) 48, (6,3) 48, (6,2) 47, (9,3) 44, (4,2) 36, (8,4) 12; 9 laws with UNKNOWN instances. Example - ((xy)x)y = (y(xx))x has models at N = 6 and 8 but none at 2, 3, 4, 5. A first run (600 laws, N <= 10, budget 2,000,000) was stopped after 22 CPU-minutes.
(xx)(xy) = y(y(yy)): models at N = 4, 6, 8 but not at N = 2
x(xy) = y(y(xx)): models at N = 5, 6, 8, 9 but not at 2, 3, 4

Divisor-closure, 150 random 3-variable laws (among the 14,223 whose affine spectrum is not all N and which survive the zero filter) and 80 random pairs of 2-variable laws, N <= 8 - 29 of the 62 laws with a model of size 2..8 violate divisor-closure, and 17 of the 34 pairs with a model; 0 UNKNOWN.

All 253 one-variable laws with <= 5 leaves per side, N <= 12, complete SAT - 213 have models of every size, 9 only N = 1, 24 violate divisor-closure (spectra missing exactly {2}, {3} or {2,3}), and the left combs x = (xx)x, x = ((xx)x)x, x = (((xx)x)x)x have spectra exactly Div(2), Div(3), Div(4); 0 UNKNOWN. H-C13-5 refuted.
x = (xx)x has spectrum exactly {1, 2} (neither {1} nor cofinite)
x = x(x(xx)) has spectrum missing exactly 2 (N <= 12)

Offset congruence closure - proves N | 3 resp. N | 2 for 16 of the 17 laws of CLM-C06-10 (not x(yz) = y((yx)z)), which with the affine models gives their exact spectra; on the whole 3-variable family it finds a bound for 7,238 of 18,581 laws (6,045 with g = 1) and proves the exact finite spectrum Div(g) for 6,912 of them (g = 1 - 6,045; 2 - 769; 3 - 84; 4 - 13; 5 - 1). Soundness test - 603 laws, 235 with a bound, 1,245 sizes not dividing the bound checked by SAT or affine models - 0 contradictions.

Lexicographic DFS (3e6 nodes) and SAT (3e5 conflicts) fail from n = 9 on, random sampling succeeds (EXP-C16-05).

new.statement: With fixed budgets, lexicographic DFS (3e6 nodes) and a SAT encoding (3e5 conflicts) find full-period quasigroups only up to n = 8, while seeded sampling of random Latin squares finds them for every n = 5..16 at rates close to 1/n^2 (H-C16-11).
new.title: Random sampling finds full-period quasigroups where exact search fails

new: All 16 magmas of order 2, all 19683 of order 3 (3330 isomorphism classes, as in OEIS A001329) and all 331776 row-permutation magmas of order 4. The maximal period of the pair map (a, b) -> (b, b*a) is n^2 for n = 2, 3, 4 (x*y = 1 - y already has period 4), refuting H-C16-1. Permutation pair maps number exactly (n!)^n (4, 216, 331776; 0 violations of the row criterion) and full-period tables exactly (n!)^n / n^2 (1, 24, 20736 - the de Bruijn counts). None of the full-period tables of order <= 4 is a quasigroup; the quasigroup maximum is n^2 - 1 (3, 8, 15). The mirror recurrence equals the forward recurrence of the transpose. The order-3 max-period distribution (4563, 4581, 5316, 2877, 1458, 540, 216, 108, 24) is not in the OEIS; the lookup of the zero counts 0, 0, 0 is vacuous.
x*y = 1 - y on {0,1}: period 4 = n^2, not a quasigroup (H-C16-1 refuted)

Exhaustive over all Latin squares of orders 2-5: no full-period quasigroup of order 2, 3, 4, exactly 3360 of order 5 (28 isomorphism classes; their left-division parastrophes are again full-period), refuting H-C16-5; an independent depth-first count of cyclic sequences with all pairs distinct at distances 1 and 2 gives the same numbers 0, 0, 0, 3360. Seeded sampling found and re-verified full-period quasigroups of every order 6-16 (isotopes of Z_n for odd n, random Latin squares for all n; hit rates roughly 1/n^2); direct products 5x6, 5x7, 5x8, 6x7, 7x8, 5x9, 7x9, 8x9 are full-period. All examples satisfy the parity condition; 2000 random isotopes of each group of order 4, 6, 8 have row-sign product (-1)^(n/2) and none is full-period, as Theorem 7 predicts.
3360 full-period quasigroups of order 5, e.g. the cycle 0,0,1,0,2,2,0,3,3,1,2,1,4,0,4,4,2,3,2,4,1,1,3,4,3 (H-C16-5 refuted)

Laver tables A_0..A_10: the pair map has exactly one fixed point and N - 1 two-cycles (maximal period 2 for n >= 1), Laver's facts used in the proof hold for every n <= 10, and the longest transient is 5 for 4 <= n <= 10. The anchored associative magma x + y + 1 has exactly the cycle structure of the Fibonacci numbers mod N (N <= 60, maximal period = Pisano period); odd-law and golden-law magmas have maximal period equal to the order of their companion matrices in every case (odd N <= 61; 51 pairs (N, a), N <= 200); 300 random affine magmas reach the order of their 3x3 affine matrix; nim-multiplication on [0,16) and [0,256) has maximal period 40 = pi(15) and 360 = pi(255). Groups: S3 8, D4 6, Q8 6, A4 16, S4 18. The odd- and golden-law period sequences are not in the OEIS (the Laver lookup 1, 2, 2, ... is a trivial match).

Simple test battery on 2^20 outputs - PCG64 passes everything; the anchored Fibonacci generator x + y + 1 on Z/2^32 and the affine magma x + beta y + 1 fail low-byte uniformity (p = 0; Fibonacci-type sequences are not uniformly distributed modulo 2^k) and their lowest bit has period 3; the LCG fails the low-bit tests (period 2, low byte too regular); the de Bruijn byte magma, whose period 65536 is the maximum possible for an order-2 byte recurrence, is too regular in every frequency test. No magma generator is competitive.

Search methods for full-period quasigroups with fixed budgets - lexicographic DFS finds a first solution for n = 5..8 (731 to 222,753 nodes) but none for n = 9, 10 within 3,000,000 nodes; the SAT encoding (CaDiCaL) solves n = 5..8 and returns UNKNOWN for n = 9, 10 after 300,000 conflicts; seeded random sampling of Latin squares succeeds for every n = 5..10 (30, 22, 21, 22, 14, 9 hits per 1500, rates close to 1/n^2). A partial DFS enumeration for n = 6 finds 1136 normalised cycles within 20,000,000 nodes without finishing.

new.statement:
For every game G on n (from n copies of F_1 to the Zeckendorf representation), |G| = B(n) - sum_{i>=2} (i-1) MC_i(G),
where B(n) = sum_i (F_{i+2} - i - 2) delta_i is the bound of Cusenza et al. and MC_i counts the combines
F_{i-1} + F_i -> F_{i+1}. Hence a game is longest iff it minimises the weighted number of such combines, and
L(n) = B(n) - D(n) with D(n) = min_G sum (i-1) MC_i(G).
new.title: Every Zeckendorf game has length B(n) - sum_{i>=2} (i-1) MC_i

new.novelty_basis: Searches (2026-10-18) for the Zeckendorf game together with lazy representations / chip-firing found no such statement; the papers on the game (Baird-Smith et al. arXiv:1809.04881; Li et al. arXiv:2006.16457; Cusenza et al. arXiv:2009.09510; Cheigh et al. 2025; Black Hole Zeckendorf games arXiv:2409.10981) do not mention lazy representations. Small; uses the classical uniqueness of lazy representations (J. L. Brown, 1965).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C19.md Theorem 2 - abelian property, an explicit carry lemma by induction, increment of the lazy representation); verified for every n < 5000 and for 300 random firing orders (EXP-C19-02); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
From n copies of F_1, every maximal sequence of split moves (F_1 + F_1 -> F_2, F_2 + F_2 -> F_1 + F_3,
F_i + F_i -> F_{i-2} + F_{i+1}) has the same length and ends at the lazy representation of n - the unique
representation as a sum of distinct F_i (F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2, ...) without two consecutive missing indices below
the largest one.
new.title: The split phase of the longest game ends at the lazy Fibonacci representation

new.novelty_basis: Cusenza et al. (2022) give the exact length only for n = F_k - 1 (their Thm 1.4) and a bound otherwise; Cheigh et al. (2025) state that a closed form for non-Fibonacci inputs is open and describe the Fibonacci case as treated by Cusenza et al., whose paper we read in full and which treats F_k - 1, not F_k. The sequence L(F_k) is not in the OEIS (EXP-C19-04). Medium-low confidence that no formula exists in the literature.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C19.md Theorem 4) from CLM-C19-01, CLM-C19-02 and the published optimality of the split-first strategy (Cusenza et al. 2022, Thm 1.2); the weight sums are Lean-verified (weight_even, weight_odd, quarter_square_even, quarter_square_odd); checked for every level j <= 33 (EXP-C19-03) and by exhaustive search for n <= 150 (EXP-C19-01); awaiting independent skeptic review
new.statement:
With F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2, F_{i+1} = F_i + F_{i-1}, the longest Zeckendorf game on n = F_k has length
F_{k+2} - k - 2 - floor((k-1)^2/4) (0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 37, 67, 117, 201, ...), i.e. its deficit to the bound
B(F_k) is the quarter-square floor((k-1)^2/4).
new.title: Closed form of the longest game on a Fibonacci number: L(F_k) = F_{k+2} - k - 2 - floor((k-1)^2/4)

new.novelty_basis: The statement is Theorem 1.4 of Cusenza et al., Fib. Quart. 60 (2022), arXiv:2009.09510; the proof via lazy representations is new to us and much shorter.
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C19.md Corollary 3, from CLM-C19-02 - a split-only game ends at the lazy representation, which equals the Zeckendorf representation exactly for alternating digit strings); consistent with EXP-C19-01 (bound attained exactly at F_k - 1 for n <= 150)
new.statement: The Zeckendorf game on n can be played with split and combine-1 moves only iff n = F_k - 1 for some k >= 2.
new.title: A short proof that only n = F_k - 1 can be played with split moves alone (Cusenza et al., Thm 1.4)

new.limitations: Inferred from all n < 30000 (in-sample) and confirmed on 6,272 further n up to 2*10^7 (out of sample); no proof. The data rely on the published optimality of the split-first strategy (confirmed independently only for n <= 150).
new.novelty_basis: Cheigh et al. (CANT VI, Springer 2025) state that a convenient closed form for the longest game on non-Fibonacci inputs is open; no such formula found in the papers above or the OEIS (L(n) has no OEIS entry, EXP-C19-04).
new.statement:
Let h(k) = floor(k^2/4) and define rho_p (p = 0, 1) by rho_p(0) = 0 and, for m = F_{i+1} + t with Zeckendorf top
level i (0 <= t < F_i): rho_p(m) = r_p(i) + [i = p mod 2] * max(0, rho_p(t) - h(i-2)), where r_p(0) = 1,
r_p(i) = h(i) + 2 for i >= 1, i = p mod 2, and r_p(i) = h(i+1) + 1 otherwise. Then D(0) = 0 and
D(F_{j+1} + m) = h(j) + D(m) - rho_{j mod 2}(m) for 0 <= m < F_j, and L(n) = B(n) - D(n).
new.title: A two-sequence recursion for the longest Zeckendorf game on every n

new.limitations: Checked for all 276 pairs with j <= 24; no proof.
new.novelty_basis: Special case of CLM-C19-05; not found in the literature searched.
new.statement:
For levels j >= i + 2, D(F_{j+1} + F_{i+1}) = floor(j^2/4) + floor(i^2/4) - R(j,i) with R(j,0) = 1,
R(j,i) = floor((i+1)^2/4) + 1 if j - i is odd and R(j,i) = floor(i^2/4) + 2 if j - i is even (i >= 1).
new.title: The deficit of a two-summand number depends only on the lower level and the parity of the gap

new.novelty_basis: Values for n <= 49 are published (Baird-Smith et al., arXiv:1809.04881, Fig. 4); optimality of the strategy for all n is Cusenza et al. 2022, Thm 1.2. Our computation is an independent check.
new.proof_check: computer-assisted - exhaustive longest-path dynamic programming over all reachable configurations (no strategy assumed), cross-checked against two independent greedy implementations and the earlier values n <= 60
new.statement: The longest game lengths L(n) for n <= 150 are those listed in results/EXP-C19-01.json (0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, ...); for every n <= 150 the split-first strategy of Cusenza et al. attains them.
new.title: Exact longest games for n <= 150 and independent confirmation of the split-first strategy

new.novelty_basis: Elementary; the reverse-move argument is used for shortest games by Cheigh et al. (2025).
new.proof_check: written proof (proofs/paper/C19.md Proposition 6 - undoing combines reaches n copies of F_1; read backwards this is a forward game); state counts equal the partition counts for every n <= 150 (EXP-C19-01)
new.statement: The positions reachable from n copies of F_1 are exactly the multisets of Fibonacci numbers F_1, F_2, ... with sum n; their number is the number of partitions of n into Fibonacci parts (OEIS A003107).
new.title: Every multiset of Fibonacci numbers with sum n is a reachable game position

new.limitations: Finite range; both statements would follow from CLM-C19-05 only with further work.
new.statement: For 1 <= n < 30000, the deficit satisfies D(n) <= floor(j^2/4) where j is the top Zeckendorf level of n (equality at the Fibonacci numbers), and L(n+1) > L(n).
new.title: D(n) <= floor(j^2/4) for top level j, and L is strictly increasing

new.counterexample: n = 12 = F_5 + F_3 + F_1 (levels 4, 2, 0): D(12) = 0 but the model gives 1; 23,680 of the n < 30000 violate it (EXP-C19-03).
new.statement: D(n) = sum_t floor(j_t^2/4) - sum_t R(j_t, j_{t+1}) over consecutive Zeckendorf levels j_1 > j_2 > ... of n.
new.title: H-C19-1: the deficit is additive up to consecutive-pair corrections (refuted)

new.counterexample: Levels (4, 2) occur with D(n) - D(n - F_5) in {0, 1} (n = 12 and n = 11); 87 such ambiguous pairs below 30000 (EXP-C19-03). The dependence is through the parity chain of lower levels, captured by rho in CLM-C19-05.
new.statement: D(n) - D(n - F_top) is a function of the two highest Zeckendorf levels of n.
new.title: H-C19-2: the effect of the top summand depends only on the two highest levels (refuted)

new.counterexample: For n < 160 the linear system D(n) = sum phi(run) has coefficient rank 46 and augmented rank 47 (exact rational elimination), so it has no solution (EXP-C19-03).
new.statement: There is a function phi(start, length) with D(n) = sum of phi over the maximal runs of ones of the lazy representation of n.
new.title: H-C19-3: the deficit is additive over the runs of the lazy representation (refuted)

new.counterexample: n = 3: L(4) = 3, L(3) = 2, lambda(3) = 0 (Zeckendorf(3) + F_1 is already Zeckendorf); fails for 288 of the first 300 n (EXP-C19-02). Longest games avoid early normalisation, so they do not pass through Zeckendorf(n).
new.statement: L(n + 1) = L(n) + lambda(n), where lambda(n) is the longest game from the Zeckendorf representation of n plus one extra F_1.
new.title: H-C19-4: the longest game is built by inserting one chip at a time (refuted)

new.improvement_detail: n = 10^7 - simulation 8.28 s, recursion 9.3e-5 s; n = 10^6 - 0.85 s vs 7.1e-5 s (CPython, loaded machine; order of magnitude only). Correctness of the recursion beyond the tested n is conjectural (CLM-C19-05); the simulation remains the reference method.
new.limitations: Conditional on CLM-C19-05.
new.novelty_basis: No sublinear method for the longest game was found in the literature listed under CLM-C19-05.
new.statement: The recursion of CLM-C19-05 evaluates L(n) with O(log^2 n) arithmetic operations; the published method (playing the split-first game) needs L(n) ~ phi^2 n moves. On the tested range both agree.
new.title: Computing the longest game in O(log^2 n) operations instead of simulating Theta(n) moves

new: Exhaustive dynamic programming (no strategy assumed) gives the longest game L(n) for every n <= 150 (up to 910,775 configurations at n = 150). It reproduces the lab's values (n <= 40), the Skeptic's (n <= 60) and hence the published ones (n <= 49); the split-first strategy of Cusenza et al. attains the optimum for every n <= 150; their bound B(n) is attained exactly for n = 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88, 143 = F_k - 1; the reachable positions are exactly the partitions of n into Fibonacci parts (OEIS A003107).

The length identity |G| = B(n) - sum_{i>=2} (i-1) MC_i holds for every greedy game n < 1500 and for 1500 uniformly random games; the split phase ends at the lazy Fibonacci representation for every n < 5000, and 300 random firing orders never change its end point or its length; the insertion hypothesis H-C19-4 fails for 288 of the first 300 n (first at n = 3).

D(F) = floor(j^2/4) for the Fibonacci input on every level j <= 33; the two-summand law holds for all 276 pairs with j <= 24; the consecutive-pair model fails for 23,680 of the n < 30000 (first n = 12), the top-summand effect is not a function of the two highest levels (87 ambiguous keys, e.g. (4,2)), and the lazy-run linear model is inconsistent already for n < 160 (rank 46 < 47); the recursion with the explicit rho reproduces D(n) for every n < 30000 (in-sample: it was inferred from this range); D(n) <= floor(j^2/4) and L(n+1) > L(n) (n >= 1) hold throughout.
H-C19-3: lazy-run model inconsistent on n < 160

Out of sample, the recursion agrees with the greedy simulation on all 6,272 tested n (every n in [30000, 36000), 200 random n < 10^6, 12 random n < 2*10^7, 60 numbers F_j + m). It evaluates L(10^7) in 9.3e-5 s against 8.3 s for the simulation. L(n), D(n), L(F_j) and the two rho sequences are not in the OEIS. (phi^2 n - L(n)) / (log_phi n)^2 stays between 0.34 and 0.38 for n = 10^3 ... 10^18.
